members.code:
structure IsRegularProjection (γ : ℝ → ℝ³) : Prop where
  immersion : ∀ t, proj (deriv γ t) ≠ 0
  finite : (crossings γ).Finite
  encard_le_two : ∀ q, (Set.range γ ∩ proj ⁻¹' {q}).encard ≤ 2
  transverse : ∀ s t, γ s ≠ γ t → proj (γ s) = proj (γ t) →
    LinearIndependent ℝ ![proj (deriv γ s), proj (deriv γ t)]
members.docstring:
The projection of `γ` to the `xy`-plane is *regular*: the projected curve is an immersion,
it has only finitely many multiple points, every multiple point is a double point (exactly two
preimages on the curve), and at every double point the two strands cross transversally.
members.meaning: Projection is an immersion with finitely many multiple points, all double and transverse.
members.name: IsRegularProjection
members.title: Ropelength problems
members.why: Different arity: the representative takes an arbitrary nonzero direction `u` and projects onto `(ℝ ∙ u)ᗮ` (with the `u ≠ 0` guard), while this variant fixes the projection to the xy-plane `x ↦ (x 0, x 1)`. Moreover the representative counts preimage *parameters* in `Set.Ico 0 1` and takes crossings as parameter pairs `(s,t)` with `0 ≤ s < t < 1`, whereas this variant counts *points* of `Set.range γ` (over all of ℝ) over a plane point and takes crossings as plane points with ≥ 2 preimages; a curve that is not injective on `[0,1)` (or not 1-periodic) is treated differently.

members.closest_existing_considered: None in Mathlib (no knot diagrams).
members.code:
structure IsRegularDiagram (γ : Circle → ℝ³) : Prop where
  contDiff : ContDiff ℝ 1 (periodicParam γ)
  immersion : ∀ t, deriv (planeProj ∘ periodicParam γ) t ≠ 0
  encard_le_two : ∀ p, (Set.range γ ∩ planeProj ⁻¹' {p}).encard ≤ 2
  finite : (crossingSet γ).Finite
  transverse : ∀ t₁ t₂, periodicParam γ t₁ ≠ periodicParam γ t₂ →
    planeProj (periodicParam γ t₁) = planeProj (periodicParam γ t₂) →
    LinearIndependent ℝ
      ![deriv (planeProj ∘ periodicParam γ) t₁, deriv (planeProj ∘ periodicParam γ) t₂]
members.docstring:
The curve `γ : Circle → ℝ³` is `C¹` and its vertical projection to the plane is a
**regular diagram**: the projected curve is an immersion, every point of the plane has at most
two preimages on the curve, there are finitely many double points, and at every double point
the two strands cross transversally.
members.meaning: The curve is C¹, its planar projection is an immersion with at most double points, finitely many of them, all transverse.
members.name: IsRegularDiagram
members.title: Ropelength and crossing number: the constant in $L(K) \geq a \operatorname{Cr}(K)^{3/4}$
members.why: Different ambient type (`γ : Circle → ℝ³` with the 2π-periodic parametrisation `t ↦ γ (Circle.exp t)`, vs `γ : ℝ → ℝ³` with period-1 parameter window `Set.Ico 0 1` and a free direction `u`), an extra `ContDiff ℝ 1` field not present in the representative, projection fixed to the xy-plane, and preimage/crossing counts are taken on `Set.range γ` (points, `encard = 2`) rather than on parameters in `[0,1)`.

groups.notes: All three are bespoke 'regular projection' predicates, but none coincide: variant 1 has an extra direction parameter u and works with parameters in [0,1); variant 2 fixes the xy-plane and counts points of the image; variant 3 uses a Circle-domain curve, adds a C¹ hypothesis, and counts image points. Mathlib has no knot-diagram notion.

groups.concept: ropelength of a curve (length divided by thickness)
labels: ropelength of a curve
ropelength of a curve (length divided by thickness)

members.closest_existing_considered: MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure 1 (used for length); eVariationOn (parametrised length, not set-based)
members.code:
noncomputable def ropelength (L : Set ℝ³) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  μH[1] L / thickness L
members.docstring:
The *ropelength* of a set `L ⊆ ℝ³`: its length (one-dimensional Hausdorff measure, which
for a link is the total length of its components) divided by its thickness. It is `∞` if `L`
has zero thickness (and positive length).
members.meaning: μH[1] L divided by thickness L in ℝ≥0∞.
members.name: ropelength
members.title: Ropelength problems

members.closest_existing_considered: None.
members.code:
noncomputable def curveRopelength (γ : ℝ → ℝ³) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ENNReal.ofReal (length γ) / ENNReal.ofReal (thickness γ)
members.docstring:
The *ropelength* of the curve `γ`: its length divided by its thickness, measured in units of
the thickness radius. It is `∞` when the thickness is `0`.
members.meaning: Length over thickness in ℝ≥0∞, ∞ when thickness is 0.
members.name: curveRopelength
members.title: Is the minimum ropelength of a knot linear in its crossing number?
members.why: Takes a parametrised curve `γ : ℝ → ℝ³` rather than a set `L : Set ℝ³`, and measures length as `∫ t in 0..1, ‖deriv γ t‖` (parametrisation-dependent, one period) instead of the Hausdorff measure `μH[1]`; its thickness is a real `iInf` (which is `0` on an empty index type) rather than an `ℝ≥0∞`-valued `iInf` (which is `⊤` when empty). Different type and different length/thickness conventions, so not interchangeable.

members.closest_existing_considered: MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure (μH[1], used for length); eVariationOn (alternative length notion, not image-based).
members.code:
noncomputable def ropelength (K : Set ℝ³) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  μH[1] K / ENNReal.ofReal (thickness K)
members.docstring:
The **ropelength** of a set `K ⊆ ℝ³` (the image of a closed curve): its length, i.e. its
one-dimensional Hausdorff measure `μH[1] K`, divided by its thickness. It is `∞` when the curve
has zero thickness (and positive length) or infinite length.
members.meaning: The one-dimensional Hausdorff measure of K divided by its thickness, in ℝ≥0∞.
members.name: ropelength
members.title: Ropelength and crossing number: the constant in $L(K) \geq a \operatorname{Cr}(K)^{3/4}$
members.why: Same type and same length `μH[1] K`, and the thickness values agree whenever `K` contains a non-collinear triple, but in the degenerate case (e.g. `K` a straight segment) variant 3's thickness is `sInf ∅ = 0` in `ℝ`, giving `ropelength K = μH[1] K / 0 = ∞`, whereas the representative's thickness is `⨅ ∅ = ⊤` in `ℝ≥0∞`, giving `ropelength L = μH[1] L / ⊤ = 0`. The two functions differ on such sets, so they are not the same object.

groups.notes: The first-listed variant is curve-based (ℝ → ℝ³) while the other two are set-based (Set ℝ³), so the set-based `RopelengthProblems.ropelength` was chosen as anchor. Variants 2 and 3 agree except on sets with no affinely independent triple (segments/lines), where the ℝ-valued `sInf ∅ = 0` convention of variant 3 flips the ropelength from 0 to ∞. Neither notion is in Mathlib.

groups.concept: ropelength of a knot type (infimum over the isotopy class)
labels: minimum ropelength of a knot type
ropelength of a knot type (infimum over the isotopy class)

members.closest_existing_considered: None.
members.code:
noncomputable def ropelength (γ : ℝ → ℝ³) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (γ' : ℝ → ℝ³) (_ : IsKnot γ') (_ : Isotopic γ γ'), curveRopelength γ'
members.docstring:
The (minimum) *ropelength* of the knot type of `γ`: the infimum of the ropelength over all
knots ambient isotopic to `γ`.
members.meaning: Infimum of curve ropelength over knots ambient isotopic to γ.
members.name: ropelength
members.title: Is the minimum ropelength of a knot linear in its crossing number?

members.closest_existing_considered: None
members.code:
noncomputable def minRopelength (L : Set ℝ³) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (L' : Set ℝ³) (_ : AmbientIsotopic L L'), ropelength L'
members.docstring:
The ropelength of the knot or link type of `L`: the infimum of the ropelength over all sets
ambient isotopic to `L`. For a tame link type this infimum is attained (Cantarella, Kusner,
Sullivan); for a wild one it is `∞`.
members.meaning: Infimum of ropelength over sets ambient isotopic to L.
members.name: minRopelength
members.title: Ropelength problems
members.why: Takes an arbitrary `Set ℝ³` rather than a periodic parametrisation `ℝ → ℝ³`, and the infimum ranges over all sets ambient isotopic to `L` (no `IsKnot`/smoothness guard), with length given by `μH[1]` instead of `∫₀¹ ‖deriv γ‖` and thickness valued in `ℝ≥0∞` (empty infimum `⊤`) rather than `ℝ` (empty infimum `0`); neither can replace the other in the other file's statement.

members.closest_existing_considered: iInf (used directly on the isotopy class).
members.code:
noncomputable def minRopelength (γ : Circle → ℝ³) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (γ' : Circle → ℝ³)
    (_ : IsEmbedding γ' ∧ AmbientIsotopic (Set.range γ) (Set.range γ')),
    ropelength (Set.range γ')
members.docstring:
The **minimum ropelength** of the knot type of the knot `γ`: the infimum of the ropelength
over all knots `γ'` whose image is ambient isotopic to that of `γ`.
members.meaning: The infimum of ropelength over embedded closed curves whose image is ambient isotopic to that of γ.
members.name: minRopelength
members.title: Ropelength and crossing number: the constant in $L(K) \geq a \operatorname{Cr}(K)^{3/4}$
members.why: Argument type is `Circle → ℝ³` rather than a 1-periodic `ℝ → ℝ³`; the infimum ranges over topological embeddings `IsEmbedding γ'` (no C¹/nonvanishing-derivative requirement) and uses `μH[1] (range γ')` for length instead of the integral `∫₀¹ ‖deriv γ'‖`; the objects are not interchangeable.

groups.notes: All three formalise 'minimum ropelength over the ambient isotopy class' but on three incompatible carriers (ℝ → ℝ³ periodic curves, Set ℝ³, Circle → ℝ³) with different notions of length (integral of ‖deriv‖ vs 1-dim Hausdorff measure), different regularity guards on the competitors (C¹ knot / none / topological embedding) and different codomains for thickness (ℝ vs ℝ≥0∞, so the empty-triple case gives 0 vs ⊤). Mathematically the infima plausibly agree on tame knots, but as Lean definitions none can be substituted for another.

groups.concept: thickness of a space curve (infimal circumradius over triples of points)
labels: thickness of a curve (infimum of circumradii of inscribed triangles)
thickness of a space curve (infimal circumradius over triples of points)

members.closest_existing_considered: Affine.Simplex.circumradius (used as the building block); Metric.infDist for a Federer-reach formulation (rejected as further from the cited source).
members.code:
noncomputable def thickness (K : Set ℝ³) : ℝ :=
  sInf {r | ∃ s : Affine.Simplex ℝ ℝ³ 2, (∀ i, s.points i ∈ K) ∧ s.circumradius = r}
members.docstring:
The **thickness** of a set `K ⊆ ℝ³`, following Gonzalez–Maddocks and [CKS02, §1]: the
infimum of the circumradii $r(x, y, z)$ over all triples of distinct points $x, y, z \in K$.
Collinear triples have $r = \infty$ and are omitted (they never contribute to the infimum). For a
`C¹` curve this equals the normal injectivity radius, i.e. the radius of the largest embedded
normal tube around the curve [CKS02, §1]; it is `0` for curves that are not `C^{1,1}`.
members.meaning: The infimum of circumradii of nondegenerate triangles with all vertices in K.
members.name: thickness
members.title: Ropelength and crossing number: the constant in $L(K) \geq a \operatorname{Cr}(K)^{3/4}$

members.closest_existing_considered: `Affine.Simplex.circumradius` (used as the building block); `Metric.infDist`/reach (not in Mathlib).
members.code:
noncomputable def thickness (γ : ℝ → ℝ³) : ℝ :=
  ⨅ s : {s : Affine.Simplex ℝ ℝ³ 2 // ∀ i, s.points i ∈ Set.range γ}, s.1.circumradius
members.docstring:
The *thickness* of the curve `γ` (Gonzalez–Maddocks, [CKS02, Section 2]): the infimum of the
circumradii of all non-degenerate triangles with vertices on the curve. Collinear triples of
points, which have infinite circumradius, do not contribute to the infimum.
members.meaning: Infimum of circumradii of nondegenerate triangles with vertices on the curve.
members.name: thickness
members.title: Is the minimum ropelength of a knot linear in its crossing number?
members.why: Same ℝ-valued infimum of circumradii over 2-simplices with vertices in the point set; the only difference is that the input is a parametrised curve `γ : ℝ → ℝ³` and the set used is `Set.range γ`, so `thickness₁ γ = thickness₃ (Set.range γ)` (iInf over the subtype is sInf of the same set of circumradii, not syntactically defeq).

members.closest_existing_considered: Affine.Simplex.circumradius (used as the building block); Metric.infDist
members.code:
noncomputable def thickness (L : Set ℝ³) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (x ∈ L) (y ∈ L) (z ∈ L) (h : AffineIndependent ℝ ![x, y, z]),
    ENNReal.ofReal (Affine.Simplex.circumradius (⟨![x, y, z], h⟩ : Affine.Simplex ℝ ℝ³ 2))
members.docstring:
The *thickness* of a set `L ⊆ ℝ³` (Gonzalez–Maddocks, Cantarella–Kusner–Sullivan):
the infimum, over all triples of distinct points `x y z ∈ L`, of the radius of the circle
through `x`, `y`, `z`. Collinear triples have circumradius `∞` and hence do not contribute to
the infimum, so it suffices to range over affinely independent triples.

For a `C^{1,1}` link this is the radius of the largest embedded normal tube around `L`, and a
curve of positive thickness is automatically `C^{1,1}`.
members.meaning: Infimum over affinely independent triples in L of the circumradius.
members.name: thickness
members.title: Ropelength problems
members.why: Codomain is `ℝ≥0∞` (via `ENNReal.ofReal`) rather than `ℝ`; in particular when `L` contains no affinely independent triple this gives `⊤` while the ℝ-valued definition gives `sInf ∅ = 0`, and even when both are nondegenerate the values live in different types and cannot be substituted for each other.

groups.notes: Chose the Set-valued, ℝ-valued variant (file 3) as anchor since it is the common denominator: variant 1 is exactly this notion precomposed with `Set.range` (curve ↦ its image), while variant 2 differs by codomain (ℝ≥0∞, with `⊤` on degenerate inputs where the ℝ-valued versions return `sInf ∅ = 0`). All three use `Affine.Simplex.circumradius` on 2-simplices with vertices in the set, excluding collinear triples.

groups.concept: tiling of euclidean space by translates of a set
labels: tiling of euclidean space by translates of a set
tiling of euclidean space by translates (disjoint interiors)

members.closest_existing_considered: `tilesByTranslation` in FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Analysis/Fourier/SpectralSets.lean — defined on `Fin d → ℝ` (not Euclidean) and measure-theoretically, so it does not combine with the Euclidean Voronoi cell; also `MeasureTheory.IsAddFundamentalDomain` (measure-theoretic, lattice-specific).
members.docstring:
A set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ *tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ by translations* if there is a set $T$ of
translation vectors such that the translates $t + P$, $t \in T$, cover $\mathbb{R}^d$ and have
pairwise disjoint interiors.
members.meaning: Some set of translation vectors gives translates covering ℝ^d with pairwise disjoint interiors.
members.name: TilesByTranslations
members.title: In parallelohedron: the Voronoi conjecture

members.closest_existing_considered: FormalConjecturesForMathlib `tilesByTranslation` (measure-theoretic, on `Fin d → ℝ`); not used because it is stated for `Fin d → ℝ` with measure-zero overlaps rather than for EuclideanSpace with disjoint interiors, and the polyhedron here lives in `ℝ³ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)`.
members.docstring:
A set `P ⊆ ℝ³` *tiles space by translation* if some family of translates of `P` covers `ℝ³`
and any two distinct translates in the family have disjoint interiors.
members.meaning: Some set of translation vectors gives translates covering ℝ³ with pairwise disjoint interiors.
members.name: TilesByTranslation
members.title: Grünbaum's conjecture on spherical polyhedra that tile space by translation
members.why: Literally the same formula (∃ T, cover = univ ∧ pairwise disjoint interiors of translates) with the ambient space fixed to ℝ³ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3); it is the d = 3 instance of the representative and the two unfold to syntactically the same term, so Iff.rfl closes it. It cannot serve for general d, which is why the general variant is the anchor.

members.closest_existing_considered: `tilesByTranslation` in FormalConjecturesForMathlib; `MeasureTheory.IsFundamentalDomain` (group-action/measure formulation, wrong shape for a general translation set T).
members.docstring:
The translates `t +ᵥ P`, `t ∈ T`, of a set `P ⊆ ℝ^d` form a **tiling** of `ℝ^d` if they
cover `ℝ^d` and have pairwise disjoint interiors.
members.meaning: The translates t + P, t ∈ T, cover ℝ^d and have pairwise disjoint interiors.
members.name: IsTilingByTranslates
members.title: Voronoi diagram: Voronoi's conjecture on parallelohedra
members.why: Takes the translation set T as an explicit argument (a predicate on the pair (P, T)) instead of existentially quantifying over T; the body coincides with the representative's matrix, so `∃ T, IsTilingByTranslates P T` is defeq to the anchor, but the stated predicate itself has a different arity/meaning (tiling by a prescribed set of translates) and cannot be substituted for a unary 'P tiles space' predicate.

groups.notes: The general-dimension variant (parallelohedron) is chosen as anchor since the first file's definition is exactly its specialisation to d = 3. Both assume the notations ℝ³ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) and ℝ^d = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d). The Voronoi variant is a binary predicate on (P, T) rather than a unary predicate on P; `∃ T, IsTilingByTranslates P T` would be defeq to the anchor, but as stated it is a different notion (tiling with a *given* translation set).

def IsTorsionFreeGroup (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ g : G, IsOfFinOrder g → g = 1
members.docstring:
A group is torsion-free if the identity is its only element of finite order.

Note that Mathlib's `IsMulTorsionFree` (injectivity of $x \mapsto x^n$ for all $n \neq 0$) is a
strictly stronger condition for non-abelian groups.
members.meaning: Every element of finite order is the identity; weaker than Mathlib's IsMulTorsionFree for non-abelian groups.
members.name: IsTorsionFreeGroup
members.title: Conjecture 10.10

members.closest_existing_considered: IsMulTorsionFree (Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Defs) — rejected because it is the unique-roots property, not torsion-freeness, for non-commutative groups; Monoid.IsTorsion (the dual notion, not applicable).
members.code:
def IsTorsionFreeGroup (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ g : G, IsOfFinOrder g → g = 1
members.docstring:
A group is *torsion-free* if its only element of finite order is the identity.

For non-commutative groups this is weaker than Mathlib's `IsMulTorsionFree`, which asks that
$x \mapsto x^k$ be injective for every $k \neq 0$ (the "unique roots" property); the two
agree for commutative groups.
members.meaning: Every element of finite order is the identity; weaker than IsMulTorsionFree for non-abelian groups.
members.name: IsTorsionFreeGroup
members.title: Conjecture 10.35
members.why: Same context (G : Type*) [Group G] and same body ∀ g : G, IsOfFinOrder g → g = 1; the why_needed prose mentions a contrapositive form but the actual code is character-for-character the same as the representative.

members.closest_existing_considered: IsMulTorsionFree (rejected as too strong for non-abelian groups; isMulTorsionFree_iff_not_isOfFinOrder requires CommGroup), Monoid.IsTorsion (the opposite notion).
members.code:
def IsTorsionFreeGroup (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ g : G, IsOfFinOrder g → g = 1
members.docstring:
A group is *torsion-free* if its only element of finite order is the identity.

This is weaker than Mathlib's `IsMulTorsionFree` (injectivity of `x ↦ x ^ n` for `n ≠ 0`), which
for non-abelian groups additionally demands uniqueness of roots.
members.meaning: Every element of finite order is the identity.
members.name: IsTorsionFreeGroup
members.title: Conjecture 8.14
members.why: Same context (G : Type*) [Group G] and same body ∀ g : G, IsOfFinOrder g → g = 1 as the representative.

groups.notes: All three files define torsion-freeness as ∀ g, IsOfFinOrder g → g = 1 on a Group. Mathlib's IsMulTorsionFree (injectivity of x ↦ x^n, n ≠ 0) is strictly stronger for non-abelian groups, so none of these is redundant with Mathlib; they are all interchangeable with each other.

groups.concept: word-representable graph
labels: word-representable graph

members.closest_existing_considered: No existing primitive; Mathlib has `SimpleGraph.lineGraph` but nothing on word-representability (checked via rg for 'WordRepresentable', 'word.represent').
members.code:
def WordRepresentable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, (∀ v, v ∈ w) ∧ ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (G.Adj x y ↔ Alternate w x y)
members.docstring:
A simple graph `G` on the vertex type `V` is *word-representable* if there is a (finite) word
`w` over the alphabet `V`, in which every vertex occurs at least once, such that two distinct
vertices `x` and `y` alternate in `w` if and only if they are adjacent in `G`.
members.meaning: Some word containing every vertex has distinct letters alternating iff adjacent in G.
members.name: WordRepresentable
members.title: Line graphs of non-word-representable graphs

members.docstring: A graph is *word-representable* if some word represents it.
members.meaning: Some word represents G.
members.name: WordRepresentable
members.title: Graphs with high representation number
members.why: Unfolding `Represents` gives exactly the representative's body; the only difference is that `Alternate`'s filter uses the `[DecidableEq V]` instance instead of `Classical.propDecidable`, which changes the `Decidable` instance term but not the proposition (Decidable is a subsingleton).

members.code:
def WordRepresentable (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, Represents w G
members.docstring: A graph is *word-representable* if some word over its vertex set represents it.
members.meaning: Some word over the vertex set represents G.
members.name: WordRepresentable
members.title: Word-representable near-triangulations
members.why: Same as the representative after unfolding `Represents`, except the biconditional is written `Alternate w x y ↔ G.Adj x y` (flipped direction) and the filter in `Alternate` uses the `[DecidableEq V]` instance rather than classical decidability; both differences are propositionally harmless.

groups.notes: All three are Kitaev's word-representability with identical `Alternate` (filter to {x,y}, IsChain (· ≠ ·)). Only difference of substance: the representative uses classical decidability for the filter (no DecidableEq V needed) while the variants use a `[DecidableEq V]` instance; the filters are propositionally but not definitionally equal, so the notions are equivalent rather than defeq. groups.concept: axiomatizable (elementary) class of groups
labels: axiomatizable (elementary) class of groups

members.closest_existing_considered: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ModelType, Theory.Model, completeTheory.
members.code:
def IsAxiomatizable (C : ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], Prop) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : groupLanguage.Theory, ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], C G ↔ G ⊨ T
members.docstring:
A class `C` of groups is *axiomatizable* if there is a set `T` of first-order sentences
in the language of groups such that `C` consists exactly of the groups that are models
of `T`.
members.meaning: There is a set of first-order sentences in the group language whose models are exactly the groups in the class.
members.name: IsAxiomatizable
members.title: Conjecture 3.20

members.closest_existing_considered: `FirstOrder.Language.Theory.Model` / `Theory.ModelType` (used as the building block; no notion of an axiomatizable class of groups exists).
members.code:
def IsFirstOrderDefinable (𝔎 : GroupClass) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : groupLanguage.Theory, ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], 𝔎 G ↔ G ⊨ T
members.docstring:
A class of groups $\mathfrak{K}$ is *definable by formulae of first-order predicate calculus*
(axiomatizable) if there is a set $T$ of sentences of the first-order language of groups such
that a group belongs to $\mathfrak{K}$ if and only if it satisfies every sentence of $T$.
members.meaning: There is a first-order theory in the group language whose models are exactly the members of the class.
members.name: IsFirstOrderDefinable
members.title: Conjecture 6.39
members.why: Both say: ∃ T : groupLanguage.Theory, ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], 𝔎 G ↔ G ⊨ T, with the same class type (GroupClass is just an abbrev for ∀ G [Group G], Prop) and structurally identical languages (function symbols mul/2, inv/1, one/0, no relations). Not defeq only because the two `GroupFunc` inductives are distinct types; transporting theories along the obvious language isomorphism (an expansion on every group under the standard interpretation) gives the equivalence.

groups.notes: Both files define the same notion (a class of groups axiomatizable by a set of first-order sentences in the language {·, ⁻¹, 1}) over exactly the same class type `∀ (G : Type) [Group G], Prop`. Neither file's `groupLanguage.Structure G` instance was supplied in the excerpt; the comparison assumes both interpret mul/inv/one as the group operations (the standard reading; any other interpretation would be a bug rather than a different notion). The `deriving Language.IsAlgebraic` on the 3.20 language is an instance, not part of the definition content, and was dropped from the check file. Mathlib has no `IsAxiomatizable`/elementary-class predicate, only `Theory.Model`/`Theory.ModelType`.

groups.concept: bi-orderable group (admits a bi-invariant linear order)
labels: bi-orderable group (admits a bi-invariant linear order)

members.closest_existing_considered: ∃ _ : LinearOrder G, MulLeftMono G ∧ MulRightMono G (equivalent; relational form chosen for uniformity with IsProOrderable). LinearOrderedCommGroup/IsOrderedMonoid rejected because they force commutativity.
members.code:
def IsOrderable (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ r : G → G → Prop, IsLinearOrder G r ∧ IsBiInvariant r
members.docstring: A group is *orderable* if it admits a bi-invariant linear order.
members.meaning: There is a linear order relation on the group invariant under left and right multiplication.
members.name: IsOrderable
members.title: Conjecture 2.28

members.closest_existing_considered: IsOrderedMonoid (commutative only), LinearOrderedCommGroup-type structures
members.code:
def IsOrderable (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ l : LinearOrder G, IsBiInvariant l.le
members.docstring: A group is *orderable* if it admits a two-sided invariant linear order.
members.meaning: There is a LinearOrder instance on G whose ≤ is bi-invariant.
members.name: IsOrderable
members.title: Conjecture 3.20
members.why: Both say G admits a linear order invariant under two-sided multiplication; 2.28 quantifies over a relation r with IsLinearOrder and one-shot invariance r a b → r (x*a*y) (x*b*y), while 3.20 quantifies over a LinearOrder structure with separate left and right invariance of ≤. A relation with IsLinearOrder yields a LinearOrder with the same ≤ (classically) and vice versa, and (x,y)-invariance is equivalent to left ∧ right invariance (take y=1 / x=1, resp. compose). Not defeq (different packaging), but provably equivalent.

groups.notes: Both variants define "bi-orderable group" (exists a bi-invariant linear order); they differ only in packaging (relation + IsLinearOrder vs LinearOrder structure; combined (x,y)-invariance vs left ∧ right invariance). Mathlib has no non-commutative version of this notion (IsOrderedMonoid/LinearOrderedCommGroup force commutativity).

groups.concept: central character of an irreducible character on a class sum
labels: central character of an irreducible character on a class sum

members.closest_existing_considered: Subgroup.centralizer / Subgroup.index (used for |K| = |G : C_G(x)|); nothing for ω_χ itself
members.code:
noncomputable def centralCharacter (χ : G → ℂ) (x : G) : ℂ :=
  ((Subgroup.centralizer {x}).index : ℂ) * χ x / χ 1
members.docstring:
The central character value $\omega_\chi(\hat K) = |K| \chi(x) / \chi(1)$ of `χ` at the
conjugacy class $K$ of `x`, where $|K| = |G : C_G(x)|$. For an irreducible character `χ` this is
an algebraic integer.
members.meaning: ω_χ(K̂) = |K|χ(x)/χ(1) with |K| the index of the centralizer of x.
members.name: centralCharacter
members.title: Conjecture 9.23

members.closest_existing_considered: IsConj, ConjClasses, finsum.
members.code:
noncomputable def centralChar (χ : G → ℂ) (g : G) : ℂ :=
  ∑ᶠ x ∈ {x : G | IsConj g x}, χ x / χ 1
members.docstring:
The value $\omega_\chi(K^+) = \sum_{x \in K} \chi(x)/\chi(1)$ of the central character of
`χ` on the class sum of the conjugacy class `K` of `g` in `G`.
members.meaning: ω_χ(K⁺) = Σ_{x∈K} χ(x)/χ(1) over the conjugacy class K of g.
members.name: centralChar
members.title: Dade's conjecture
members.why: Both take an arbitrary function χ : G → ℂ, but the representative uses only the single value χ x scaled by |G : C_G(x)|, whereas the variant sums χ over the whole conjugacy class of g (finsum over {x | IsConj g x}, Mathlib's IsConj on G). These agree exactly when χ is constant on the class (e.g. any class function / irreducible character, also in the infinite-index case where both give 0), but differ for general χ: in S₃ with χ = indicator of {1, a} for a transposition a, the representative gives 3 at a while the variant gives 1. (Also Type vs Type* universe.)

groups.notes: The two definitions coincide on class functions (hence on all characters, the only intended inputs), so within the conjecture statements they are interchangeable; as definitions on arbitrary G → ℂ they are not equal.

groups.concept: centrally nilpotent loop
labels: centrally nilpotent loop

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib `upperCentralSeries`/`Group.IsNilpotent`/`Subgroup.center` — group-only, cannot be applied to loops.
members.code:
def IsCentrallyNilpotent (L : Type*) [Loop L] : Prop :=
  ∃ n : ℕ, upperCentralSeries L n = Set.univ
members.docstring:
A loop is centrally nilpotent (in the sense of Bruck) if its upper central series reaches
the whole loop after finitely many steps.
members.meaning: A loop whose upper central series reaches the whole loop in finitely many steps (Bruck).
members.name: IsCentrallyNilpotent
members.title: Conjecture 8.4

members.closest_existing_considered: `Group.IsNilpotent`, `IsSolvable`, `QuotientGroup` (groups only).
members.code: def IsNilpotent (Q : Type u) [Loop Q] : Prop := ∃ n, IsNilpotentOfClassLE n Q
members.docstring: A loop is (centrally) *nilpotent* if it is nilpotent of some finite class.
members.meaning: The loop is centrally nilpotent of some finite class.
members.name: IsNilpotent
members.title: Problems in loop theory and quasigroup theory
members.why: Mathematically both express 'Q is centrally nilpotent of some finite class': Variant 1 says Z_n(L) = L for the upper central series (Z_0 = {1}, Z_{n+1} = preimage of Z(L/Z_n) coded via a ∈ b·Z_n, valid since each Z_n is a normal subloop); Variant 2 is the recursive form 'Q trivial' / 'Q/Z(Q) (any surjective mul-hom image with kernel Z(Q), unique up to iso) has class ≤ n', and Z_n(Q/Z(Q)) = Z_{n+1}(Q)/Z(Q) identifies them. However the two files use distinct bespoke `Loop` classes (equational with two divisions vs MulOneClass with bijective translations), so neither can literally replace the other, and a formal equivalence proof would require bridging instances plus the quotient-loop construction, which I could not carry out to certify the check; hence marked unclear rather than verified equivalent.

groups.notes: I believe the two definitions agree mathematically (Bruck central nilpotency: ∃ n, Z_n = L ⇔ ∃ n, class ≤ n), but they are stated over two different bespoke `Loop` classes (Kourovka: (·,\,/,1) equational axioms; WP: MulOneClass + bijective translations). A verified Lean equivalence would need an instance bridge, construction of quotient loops by normal subloops, and the lemma Z_n(Q/Z(Q)) = Z_{n+1}(Q)/Z(Q); this was beyond what could be produced and checked here, so the verdict is 'unclear' with a strong expectation of equivalence. Neither notion is in Mathlib (no loop theory there).

groups.concept: centre of a loop
labels: centre of a loop

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib `upperCentralSeries`/`Group.IsNilpotent`/`Subgroup.center` — group-only, cannot be applied to loops.
members.docstring:
The centre of the loop `L`: the elements that commute with every element and associate
with every pair of elements in every position, i.e. the intersection of the nucleus with the
commutant.
members.meaning: Elements commuting with every element and associating with every pair in every position (nucleus ∩ commutant).
members.name: center
members.title: Conjecture 8.4

members.closest_existing_considered: `Subgroup`, `Subgroup.Normal`, `frattini` (groups only), `Subgroup.center`.
members.docstring: The *center* `Z(Q)` of a loop: the elements that commute and associate with all elements.
members.meaning: Elements commuting with all elements and associating with every pair in every position.
members.name: center
members.title: Problems in loop theory and quasigroup theory
members.why: Identical predicate (commute with all x and associate with all x,y in all three positions), depending only on `*`; the two `Loop` classes are equivalent axiomatizations (equational divisions vs bijective translations) inducing the same Mul/One, so the centres coincide by `rfl` once the instance is transported.

groups.notes: Both files define the centre by the literally same set-builder predicate (commute with every x, and associate in all three positions with every pair x,y), which only depends on the multiplication. The only difference is the ambient `Loop` class: Kourovka uses the equational signature (*, 1, ⧵, /) with the four division axioms, the WP file uses `MulOneClass` plus bijectivity of left/right translations. These are the two standard, mutually equivalent axiomatizations of a loop (divisions are uniquely determined by multiplication), and the centre is definitionally the same after transporting the instance either way. The types cannot be substituted syntactically without transporting the `Loop` instance, but the mathematical notion is the same.

groups.concept: chernikov group
labels: chernikov group

members.closest_existing_considered: WellFoundedLT (Subgroup G) alone (too weak: min-groups need not be Chernikov, e.g. Tarski monsters), Subgroup.FiniteIndex + IsMulCommutative alone (too weak: virtually abelian without min, e.g. ℤ); a Prüfer-group model via rootsOfUnity/AddCircle (would add more bespoke, less checkable definitions).
members.code:
def IsChernikov (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ A : Subgroup G, A.FiniteIndex ∧ IsMulCommutative A ∧ WellFoundedLT (Subgroup A)
members.docstring:
A group is a *Chernikov group* if it has an abelian subgroup of finite index that
satisfies the minimal condition on subgroups (every non-empty set of subgroups has a minimal
element, i.e. `<` on subgroups is well-founded).

By Kurosh's theorem, an abelian group satisfies the minimal condition on subgroups exactly
when it is the direct product of a finite group and finitely many quasicyclic (Prüfer)
groups. Hence this is equivalent to the usual definition of a Chernikov group as a finite
extension of a direct product of finitely many quasicyclic groups.
members.meaning: There is an abelian subgroup of finite index satisfying the minimal condition on subgroups (well-founded < on its subgroups).
members.name: IsChernikov
members.title: Conjecture 10.77

members.closest_existing_considered: Group.IsVirtuallyNilpotent (Mathlib.GroupTheory.Nilpotent) is the closest existing 'virtually P' predicate but has the wrong P and lacks the Min condition; WellFoundedLT (Subgroup G) and Subgroup.FiniteIndex / IsMulCommutative are the existing primitives the definition is built from. Mathlib's only Prüfer-related content (Dynamics/FixedPoints/Prufer.lean) is a lemma, not a definition of the Prüfer group.
members.code:
def IsChernikov (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  (∃ N : Subgroup G, N.FiniteIndex ∧ IsMulCommutative N) ∧ WellFoundedLT (Subgroup G)
members.docstring:
A group $G$ is a *Chernikov group* if it is a finite extension of a direct product of finitely
many Prüfer (quasicyclic) $p$-groups. By Kurosh's theorem on abelian groups with the minimal
condition (see D. J. S. Robinson, *A Course in the Theory of Groups*, Sections 4.2 and 5.4),
this holds if and only if $G$ has an abelian subgroup of finite index and satisfies the minimal
condition on subgroups, that is, there is no infinite strictly descending chain of subgroups
of $G$. We use this characterisation as the definition. In particular every finite group is
Chernikov.
members.meaning: The group has an abelian subgroup of finite index and satisfies the minimal condition on subgroups (WellFoundedLT on Subgroup G).
members.name: IsChernikov
members.title: Conjecture 10.78
members.why: Both say 'virtually abelian + minimal condition on subgroups', but 10.77 puts WellFoundedLT on the lattice of subgroups of the finite-index abelian subgroup A while 10.78 puts it on Subgroup G. These are logically equivalent (Min passes to subgroups, and lifts from a finite-index subgroup since |H : H ∩ A| ≤ |G : A| is finite) but not definitionally equal; a real proof is required.

groups.notes: Both files use the same characterisation 'abelian-by-finite with the minimal condition on subgroups' (neither Chernikov nor Prüfer groups are in Mathlib). The only difference is whether Min is required of the finite-index abelian subgroup or of the whole group; these are provably equivalent (Min is inherited by subgroups and is closed under finite extensions), so the two definitions are interchangeable, though not definitionally equal.

groups.concept: christoffel symbols of the second kind (levi-civita connection in a chart)
labels: christoffel symbols of the second kind (levi-civita connection in a chart)

members.closest_existing_considered: ContinuousLinearMap.inverse (used for raising the index); no connection exists in Mathlib.
members.code:
noncomputable def christoffel (x₀ : M) (y : E) (u v : E) : E :=
  (metricCoord I x₀ y).inverse (christoffelFirst I x₀ y u v)
members.docstring:
The Christoffel symbols of the second kind in the chart `extChartAt I x₀`: the coordinate
vector `Γ(u, v) = ∇ᵤ v` characterised by `g(Γ(u, v), w) = christoffelFirst I x₀ y u v w` for all
`w`. It is obtained by inverting the metric coefficients; `ContinuousLinearMap.inverse` is the
genuine inverse because `metricCoord I x₀ y` is a linear isomorphism `E ≃ E*` for `y` in the
open target of the chart.
members.meaning: The coordinate vector Γ(u,v)=∇ᵤv obtained by inverting the metric coefficients applied to the Christoffel symbols of the first kind.
members.name: christoffel
members.title: Quantum unique ergodicity for eigenfunctions of the Laplacian
variables:
variable
  {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]
  {H : Type*} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H)
  {M : Type*} [EMetricSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M]
  [RiemannianBundle (fun (x : M) ↦ TangentSpace I x)]

members.closest_existing_considered: Nothing in Mathlib: no `Connection`, `LeviCivita`, `Christoffel`, or `covariantDeriv`.
members.code:
noncomputable def christoffel (p : M) (y : E) (v w : E) : E :=
  let dg := fderiv ℝ (metricInChart I p) y
  (metricInChart I p y).inverse ((1 / 2 : ℝ) • (dg v w + dg w v - (dg.flip v).flip w))
members.docstring:
The Christoffel symbols of the Levi-Civita connection in the chart at `p`, packaged as a
bilinear map: `christoffel I p y v w` is the covariant derivative `∇ᵥ w` at the chart coordinate
`y` of the constant coordinate vector fields `v` and `w`. It is determined by the Koszul formula
`2 g(∇ᵥ w, z) = ∂ᵥ g(w, z) + ∂_w g(v, z) - ∂_z g(v, w)`, where `g` is the metric in the chart.
members.meaning: ∇ᵥw for constant coordinate fields via the Koszul formula, inverting the metric coefficients.
members.name: christoffel
members.title: Hopf conjecture
variables:
variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  {H : Type*} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H)
  {M : Type*} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M] [IsManifold I 1 M]
  [RiemannianBundle (fun x : M ↦ TangentSpace I x)]
members.why: The Koszul/inversion step is literally the same (½(D u v + D v u − (D.flip u).flip v), then ContinuousLinearMap.inverse of the metric), but the metric coefficients differ: Eigenfunction pulls back ⟪·,·⟫ along `mfderiv 𝓘(ℝ,E) I (extChartAt I x₀).symm y` (which is `fderiv` on all of E of the transition map, and is 0 where not MDifferentiableAt, e.g. at boundary points or outside the chart target), whereas Hopf uses `(trivializationAt E (TangentSpace I) p).symmL ℝ x` = `fderivWithin … (range I)` of the same transition map, which is 0 whenever x ∉ chart source. These agree for y in the chart target of a boundaryless model with `IsManifold I 1 M`, but not as total functions (boundary points, y outside the target), and the ambient hypotheses differ (Hopf needs `IsManifold I 1 M` for the tangent-bundle trivialization; Eigenfunction needs `FiniteDimensional ℝ E` and `EMetricSpace M` and no manifold structure), so neither can replace the other verbatim.

groups.notes: Both are the standard coordinate Christoffel symbols Γ(u,v)=∇ᵤv via the Koszul formula with index raised by inverting the metric matrix; the only mathematical divergence is how the metric coefficients in the chart are extracted (mfderiv of the inverse chart vs symmL of the tangent bundle trivialization), which coincide on the interior of the chart target under IsManifold I 1 M but differ as total functions and in required instances. Mathlib has no Levi-Civita connection or Christoffel symbols.

members.why: Representative returns unordered pairs of distinct parameters (s,t) in [0,1) whose projections along an arbitrary direction u coincide; the variant returns points q of the xy-plane (fixed projection, no u) with at least two preimages in Set.range γ, counting distinct space points rather than parameters and with no period window. Different objects and different ambient data.

groups.concept: curl of a vector field on ℝ³
labels: curl of a vector field on ℝ³

members.closest_existing_considered: Searched Mathlib for 'curl' (nothing); considered expressing components inline with fderiv, but a named definition with tests is clearer.
members.code:
noncomputable def curl (v : ℝ³ → ℝ³) (x : ℝ³) : ℝ³ :=
  let D : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℝ := fun j i => fderiv ℝ v x (EuclideanSpace.single j 1) i
  !₂[D 1 2 - D 2 1, D 2 0 - D 0 2, D 0 1 - D 1 0]
members.docstring:
The curl $\nabla \times v$ of a vector field $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ at a
point $x$, with components $\partial_2 v_3 - \partial_3 v_2$, $\partial_3 v_1 - \partial_1 v_3$
and $\partial_1 v_2 - \partial_2 v_1$. Here $\partial_j v_i$ is the `i`-th component of
`fderiv ℝ v x` applied to the `j`-th standard basis vector. The curl of the velocity field of a
fluid is its vorticity.
If `v` is not differentiable at `x`, then `fderiv` is the zero map and the curl is `0`.
members.meaning: ∇ × v computed from fderiv components (0 where not differentiable).
members.name: curl
members.title: Regularity of solutions of the Euler equations

members.closest_existing_considered: None in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib; defined in coordinates mirroring `cross_apply`.
members.code:
noncomputable def curl (F : ℝ³ → ℝ³) (x : ℝ³) : ℝ³ :=
  WithLp.toLp 2 ![partialDeriv F x 1 2 - partialDeriv F x 2 1,
    partialDeriv F x 2 0 - partialDeriv F x 0 2,
    partialDeriv F x 0 1 - partialDeriv F x 1 0]
members.docstring:
The curl
$\nabla \times F = (\partial_1 F_2 - \partial_2 F_1,\ \partial_2 F_0 - \partial_0 F_2,\
\partial_0 F_1 - \partial_1 F_0)$ of a vector field $F : \mathbb R^3 \to \mathbb R^3$ at `x`,
with coordinates indexed by `0, 1, 2`.
members.meaning: ∇ × F at x computed from partial derivatives.
members.name: curl
members.title: Regularity of solutions of the Vlasov–Maxwell equations
members.why: Same components in the same order with the same index convention (partialDeriv F x j i = fderiv ℝ F x (EuclideanSpace.single j 1) i = the representative's D j i), packed via WithLp.toLp 2 ![...] which is exactly the !₂[...] notation; the only differences are a local `let` vs an auxiliary def, so the two unfold to syntactically the same term.

groups.notes: Both are the standard coordinate curl on EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) built from fderiv applied to standard basis vectors; Mathlib has no curl, so a bespoke definition is justified. The two are interchangeable.

groups.concept: decidable first-order theory
labels: decidable first-order theory

members.closest_existing_considered: `ComputablePred` (requires a `Primcodable` instance on sentences, which does not exist); `FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsComplete`/`IsSatisfiable` (different notions).
members.code:
def IsDecidableTheory (T : L.Theory) : Prop :=
  ∃ f : ℕ → Bool, Computable f ∧ ∀ φ : L.Sentence, f (godelNumber φ) = true ↔ φ ∈ T
members.docstring:
An `L`-theory `T` (a set of `L`-sentences) is *decidable* if there is a computable function
`f : ℕ → Bool` which, applied to the Gödel number of any sentence `φ`, returns `true` if and
only if `φ ∈ T`.
members.meaning: There is a computable ℕ → Bool that on Gödel numbers returns true exactly for sentences in T.
members.name: IsDecidableTheory
members.title: Decidability of the theory of $\mathbb{F}_p((t))$
variables: variable {L : Language} [Encodable (Σ i, L.Functions i)] [Encodable (Σ i, L.Relations i)]

members.closest_existing_considered: `ComputablePred` directly on `L.Sentence` (impossible: no `Primcodable L.Sentence`); `Theory.IsComplete`/`IsSatisfiable` (different notions).
members.code:
def Theory.IsDecidable {L : Language} [Encodable (Σ n, L.Functions n)]
    [Encodable (Σ n, L.Relations n)] (T : L.Theory) : Prop :=
  ComputablePred (· ∈ Sentence.godelNumber '' T)
members.docstring:
A theory `T` (in a language with encodable symbols) is *decidable* if the set of Gödel
numbers of the sentences in `T` is a computable set of natural numbers.
members.meaning: The set of Gödel numbers of sentences of T is a computable predicate on ℕ.
members.name: Theory.IsDecidable
members.title: Tarski's exponential function problem
members.why: Same Gödel numbering, but the variant requires `ComputablePred` of the image set, so the decider must return `false` on all non-Gödel-numbers; the representative only constrains `f` on Gödel numbers of sentences. Variant ⇒ representative holds (listEncode injective), but the converse fails: for `T = Set.univ` the representative is trivially true while the variant requires the range of `godelNumber` to be computable, which is false for a pathological `Encodable (Σ i, L.Functions i)` whose `encode` has non-computable range (only `Encodable`, not `Primcodable`, is assumed).

groups.notes: The variant is strictly stronger in general; they agree exactly when `Set.range godelNumber` is a computable subset of ℕ (which is not provable from the `Encodable` hypotheses alone and is not established in Mathlib even for Primcodable symbols).

groups.concept: elementary subgroup e_n(r) generated by elementary transvections
labels: elementary subgroup e_n(r) generated by elementary transvections

members.closest_existing_considered: Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Mathlib) as the ambient group; Subgroup.closure for generation. No existing elementary subgroup definition in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib.
members.docstring:
The elementary subgroup $E_m(R)$: the subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_m(R)$ generated by the
transvections $1 + c\,e_{ij}$, $i \neq j$.
members.meaning: The subgroup of SL_m(R) (commutative R) generated by all elementary transvections 1 + c e_ij, i ≠ j.
members.name: elementarySubgroup
members.title: Conjecture 10.38

members.closest_existing_considered: Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.diagonalSubgroup (FormalConjecturesForMathlib), Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (both unrelated / commutative)
members.code:
def elementarySubgroup : Subgroup (GL (Fin n) R) :=
  Subgroup.closure {g | ∃ (i j : Fin n) (hij : i ≠ j) (a : R), g = elementaryTransvection hij a}
members.docstring:
The elementary subgroup $E_n(R)$ of $GL_n(R)$: the subgroup generated by all elementary
transvections $t_{ij}(a)$ with $i \ne j$ and $a \in R$.
members.meaning: The subgroup of GL_n(R) (R any ring) generated by all elementary transvections t_ij(a), i ≠ j.
members.name: elementarySubgroup
members.title: Conjecture 10.45
members.why: The representative is a `Subgroup (SpecialLinearGroup m R)` for an arbitrary finite index type `m` and a `CommRing R`, whereas this variant is a `Subgroup (GL (Fin n) R)` over a possibly noncommutative `Ring R` with index type `Fin n`; the ambient group (SL vs GL), ring hypothesis and index type all differ, so neither can replace the other in the other file's statement (they only agree mathematically up to the embedding SL_n(R) ↪ GL_n(R) when R is commutative and m = Fin n).

groups.notes: Both are Subgroup.closure of the set of transvections 1 + a·e_{ij} (i ≠ j), but as Lean objects they are subgroups of different groups (SL_m(R) vs GL_n(R)) with different generality (CommRing vs Ring, arbitrary Fintype m vs Fin n). Mathlib has no E_n(R); Matrix.transvection exists only as a matrix, not as a subgroup.

groups.concept: evaluation of a loop term under a variable assignment
labels: evaluation of a loop term under a variable assignment

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib `FreeMagma` (only one binary operation, no constant or division symbols); `FirstOrder.Language.Term` (heavier model-theoretic machinery; no ready loop language).
members.code:
def LoopTerm.eval {α : Type*} [LoopSignature α] (v : ℕ → α) : LoopTerm → α
  | var n => v n
  | one => 1
  | mul s t => s.eval v * t.eval v
  | ldiv s t => s.eval v ⧵ t.eval v
  | rdiv s t => s.eval v / t.eval v
members.docstring:
The value of a term in an algebra `α` of the loop signature under an assignment `v` of the
variables.
members.meaning: The value of a loop term in an algebra of the loop signature given values for the variables.
members.name: LoopTerm.eval
members.title: Conjecture 8.4

members.closest_existing_considered: `FreeMagma`, `FreeGroup`, `FreeMonoid` (wrong variety; no divisions), `FirstOrder.Language.Term` (heavier model-theory machinery, no loop signature).
members.code:
def eval (f : α → Q) : Term α → Q
  | var a => f a
  | one => 1
  | mul s t => eval f s * eval f t
  | ldiv s t => eval f s ⧵ eval f t
  | div s t => eval f s / eval f t
members.docstring: Evaluate a term in a loop `Q` under an assignment `f` of the variables.
members.meaning: The value of a loop term in a loop given values for the variables.
members.name: eval
members.title: Problems in loop theory and quasigroup theory
members.why: The representative evaluates `LoopTerm` (variables indexed by ℕ) in an arbitrary axiom-free `LoopSignature α` where `ldiv` is a primitive operation, whereas the variant evaluates `Term α` (variables from an arbitrary `α : Type`) only in a bespoke `Loop Q` (with loop axioms) where `ldiv` is derived as the inverse of left multiplication; different term type, different variable index type, and different ambient structure.

groups.notes: Neither is in Mathlib. The two term types themselves differ (ℕ-indexed vs α-indexed variables), and the evaluation targets differ (axiom-free signature vs actual Loop class), so no direct equivalence statement is even well-typed without a translation of terms and a coercion of Loop to LoopSignature.

groups.concept: exterior derivative of a 1-form on a manifold
labels: exterior derivative of a 1-form on a manifold (computed in charts)
exterior derivative of a 1-form on a manifold (invariant formula)

members.closest_existing_considered: `extDeriv`, `extDerivWithin` (Mathlib.Analysis.Calculus.DifferentialForm.Basic), whose TODO explicitly says manifold versions are not defined yet.
members.code:
noncomputable def extDerivOneForm (α : (z : N) → TangentSpace I z →L[ℝ] ℝ) (z : N)
    (u w : TangentSpace I z) : ℝ :=
  extDerivWithin
    (fun y : E ↦ ContinuousAlternatingMap.ofSubsingleton ℝ E ℝ (0 : Fin 1)
      ((α ((extChartAt I z).symm y)).comp (mfderiv 𝓘(ℝ, E) I (extChartAt I z).symm y)))
    (extChartAt I z).target (extChartAt I z z)
    ![mfderiv I 𝓘(ℝ, E) (extChartAt I z) z u, mfderiv I 𝓘(ℝ, E) (extChartAt I z) z w]
members.docstring:
The exterior derivative $d\alpha$ of a $1$-form `α` on a manifold `N`, evaluated at `z` on
the tangent vectors `u`, `w`. It is computed in the chart $e = $ `extChartAt I z`: the coordinate
expression of `α` is the $1$-form $\tilde\alpha(y) = \alpha_{e^{-1}(y)} \circ d(e^{-1})_y$ on
the model space, whose exterior derivative (`extDerivWithin`, within the target of $e$) is
evaluated at $e(z)$ on the images of `u`, `w` under $de_z$. For a differentiable `α` and a
boundaryless manifold this does not depend on the chart, by naturality of the exterior
derivative.
members.meaning: dα at z on tangent vectors u, w, computed via extDerivWithin of the coordinate expression of α in extChartAt.
members.name: extDerivOneForm
members.title: Nearby Lagrangian conjecture
variables:
variable {E H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [TopologicalSpace H]
  (I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H) {N : Type*} [TopologicalSpace N] [ChartedSpace H N]

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib `extDeriv` (normed spaces only, not manifolds).
members.code:
noncomputable def extDerivOneForm (α : Π x : M, TangentSpace I x →L[ℝ] ℝ)
    (X Y : SmoothVectorField I M) (x : M) : ℝ :=
  vectorFieldDeriv I X (fun y ↦ α y (Y y)) x - vectorFieldDeriv I Y (fun y ↦ α y (X y)) x
    - α x (mlieBracket I X Y x)
members.docstring:
The exterior derivative of a `1`-form `α`, evaluated at `x` on the smooth vector fields `X`
and `Y`, via the invariant formula `dα(X, Y) = X(α(Y)) - Y(α(X)) - α([X, Y])`.
members.meaning: dα(X,Y)=X(α(Y))−Y(α(X))−α([X,Y]) evaluated at a point on smooth vector fields.
members.name: extDerivOneForm
members.title: Weinstein conjecture
members.why: The representative is a pointwise bilinear form dα_z(u,w) on tangent vectors, computed via extDerivWithin in the chart extChartAt (no IsManifold assumption, chart-dependent for non-smooth α); the variant takes two global smooth vector fields X Y and a point, defined by the invariant formula X(α(Y)) − Y(α(X)) − α([X,Y]) with mfderiv/mlieBracket under [IsManifold I ∞ M]. Different argument types and hypotheses; their agreement (dα_x(X x, Y x) = invariant formula) is a nontrivial theorem valid only for differentiable α on boundaryless manifolds, not an equivalence of definitions.

groups.notes: Both are bespoke because Mathlib's extDeriv/extDerivWithin exist only on normed spaces. The two approaches (chart-based pointwise vs. invariant Cartan formula on vector fields) are mathematically compatible for smooth 1-forms on boundaryless manifolds, but as Lean definitions they have different signatures and hypotheses and cannot be substituted for one another.

groups.concept: facet of a 3-dimensional convex polytope (exposed face of dimension 2)
labels: facet of a 3-dimensional convex polytope (exposed face of dimension 2)
facet of a convex polyhedron in ℝ³

members.closest_existing_considered: `IsExposed` (used, together with `affineSpan`/`finrank` to select 2-dimensional exposed sets).
members.code:
def IsFacet (Q F : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  IsExposed ℝ Q F ∧ Module.finrank ℝ (affineSpan ℝ F).direction = 2
members.docstring:
`F` is a *facet* (a two-dimensional face) of the convex polyhedron `Q`: an exposed subset
of `Q` whose affine span is a plane.
members.meaning: An exposed subset of Q whose affine span is 2-dimensional.
members.name: IsFacet
members.title: Grünbaum's conjecture on spherical polyhedra that tile space by translation

members.closest_existing_considered: `IsExposed` and `IsExtreme` (Mathlib.Analysis.Convex.Exposed / Extreme); `IsExtreme` alone was rejected because extreme subsets need not be convex (e.g. a set of several vertices), so `IsExposed` plus the dimension condition is used.
members.code:
def IsFacet (K F : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  IsExposed ℝ K F ∧ Module.finrank ℝ (vectorSpan ℝ F) = 2
members.docstring:
`IsFacet K F` means that `F` is a facet (a two-dimensional face) of the convex polytope
`K ⊆ ℝ³`: `F` is an exposed face of `K` whose affine span is a plane.
members.meaning: F is an exposed face of K ⊆ ℝ³ whose vector span has dimension exactly 2.
members.name: IsFacet
members.title: Shephard's problem (a.k.a. Dürer's conjecture)
members.why: Same IsExposed ℝ K F conjunct; the dimension condition uses `vectorSpan ℝ F` instead of `(affineSpan ℝ F).direction`. These are propositionally equal by `direction_affineSpan` but not definitionally (direction of affineSpan unfolds to `vectorSpan ℝ (spanPoints ℝ F)`), so the notions coincide but are not defeq.

groups.notes: Both encode a facet as an exposed subset of the polytope with 2-dimensional affine hull. The ℝ³ notation is assumed to denote the same type in both files (the check uses EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)); the equivalence proof does not depend on the particular choice of ambient 3-space.

members.code:
structure FinitePresentation where
  /-- The number of generators. -/
  numGenerators : ℕ
  /-- The relators, as words in the generators and their inverses. -/
  relators : List (List (Fin numGenerators × Bool))
members.docstring:
A finite group presentation $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid r_1, \dots, r_k \rangle$: a number
`n` of generators together with a finite list of relators, each a word in the letters
$x_i^{\pm 1}$. As in `FreeGroup.mk`, the letter `(i, true)` stands for $x_i$ and the letter
`(i, false)` stands for $x_i^{-1}$.
members.meaning: A natural number of generators together with a list of words in the generators and inverses as relators.
members.name: FinitePresentation
members.title: Conjecture 7.21

members.closest_existing_considered: PresentedGroup, FreeGroup.mk, Primcodable.list/prod/fin, BranchingVAS.Bvas (repo idiom of a structure with a Primcodable instance via ofEquiv)
members.code:
structure FinitePresentation where
  /-- The number $n$ of generators $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$. -/
  numGenerators : ℕ
  /-- The finite list of relators, each a word in the letters $x_i^{\pm 1}$. -/
  relators : List (List (ℕ × Bool))
  /-- Every letter of every relator refers to one of the generators. -/
  letter_lt : ∀ w ∈ relators, ∀ l ∈ w, l.1 < numGenerators
members.docstring:
A finite group presentation $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid R \rangle$.
A letter `(i, b)` of a relator stands for $x_i$ if `b = true` and for $x_i^{-1}$ if
`b = false`, following the convention of `FreeGroup.mk`.
members.meaning: A number of generators together with a finite list of relator words whose letters index the generators.
members.name: FinitePresentation
members.title: Conjecture 9.53
members.why: Both record a number n of generators and a finite list of relator words over letters x_i^{±1} with the FreeGroup.mk (i, Bool) convention; 7.21 types the letters as Fin n × Bool, while 9.53 uses ℕ × Bool plus a proof that every letter index is < n (chosen only to get a Primcodable instance). The two structures are not definitionally equal but are canonically in bijection (forget/reattach the bound on each letter), so they carry exactly the same data.

groups.notes: Both are Type-valued structures, so "equivalence" here means a canonical bijection (Equiv), not a Prop-iff: (n, relators over Fin n × Bool) ↔ (n, relators over ℕ × Bool, proof all indices < n). The 9.53 encoding is chosen purely for Primcodable convenience; the presented group (PresentedGroup on Fin n via FreeGroup.mk) is the same for both. Neither notion exists in Mathlib.

groups.concept: finitely based equational theory of a loop-signature algebra
labels: finitely based equational theory of a loop-signature algebra

members.closest_existing_considered: Nothing in Mathlib or the repo about varieties/equational theories/finitely based laws.
members.code:
def LoopSignature.HasFiniteBasis (α : Type*) [LoopSignature α] : Prop :=
  ∃ S : Set LoopLaw, S.Finite ∧ ∀ e, LoopLaw.IsConsequence S e ↔ e ∈ LoopSignature.laws α
members.docstring:
The laws of `α` have a finite basis: there is a finite set `S` of laws whose equational
consequences are exactly the laws of `α`.
members.meaning: There is a finite set of laws whose equational consequences are exactly the laws of the algebra.
members.name: LoopSignature.HasFiniteBasis
members.title: Conjecture 8.4

members.closest_existing_considered: `FreeMagma`, `FreeGroup`, `FreeMonoid` (wrong variety; no divisions), `FirstOrder.Language.Term` (heavier model-theory machinery, no loop signature).
members.code:
def HasFiniteBasisOfLaws (Q : Type u) [Loop Q] : Prop :=
  ∃ B : Finset (Term ℕ × Term ℕ), (∀ p ∈ B, IsLaw Q p.1 p.2) ∧
    ∀ s t : Term ℕ, IsLaw Q s t →
      ∀ (R : Type) [Loop R], (∀ p ∈ B, IsLaw R p.1 p.2) → IsLaw R s t
members.docstring:
The laws of `Q` have a *finite basis* if there is a finite set `B` of laws of `Q` such that
every law of `Q` holds in every loop satisfying all identities in `B` (i.e. is a consequence
of `B`).
members.meaning: A finite set of laws of Q such that every law of Q holds in every loop satisfying them.
members.name: HasFiniteBasisOfLaws
members.title: Problems in loop theory and quasigroup theory
members.why: Different ambient structure and different consequence relation: the representative is a predicate on arbitrary `LoopSignature` algebras (no axioms) and takes equational consequence over all loop-signature algebras, whereas the variant is a predicate on genuine `Loop`s (MulOneClass with bijective translations, divisions derived from the axioms) and takes consequence only over all loops (i.e. relative to the variety of loops). The two cannot even be stated on the same type without a bridge between the type classes; their agreement for actual loops is a nontrivial theorem (loops are finitely axiomatized by identities), not a definitional or straightforward equivalence.

groups.notes: Both encode 'the identities of a loop are finitely based' (Kourovka 8.4 / Evans-type question), but one works absolutely in the loop signature over all signature algebras, the other relatively within the variety of loops with `Loop` as the ambient class. For an honest loop these agree mathematically only because the loop variety is finitely based, and the shapes of the definitions (∃ finite S, Cn(S) = Laws vs ∃ finite B ⊆ Laws, Laws ⊆ Cn_loops(B)) are otherwise equivalent.

groups.concept: genus of a function field (algebraic curve)
labels: genus of a function field (algebraic curve)

members.closest_existing_considered: None (no genus in Mathlib).
members.code:
noncomputable def genus : ℕ :=
  sSup {g : ℕ | ∃ D : Divisor F, (g : ℤ) = D.deg - D.ell + 1}
members.docstring:
The genus of the curve with function field `F`, defined via Riemann's theorem as
`g = max {deg D - ℓ(D) + 1 | D a divisor}` (see [St09, Section 1.4]).
members.meaning: max{deg D − ℓ(D) + 1} over divisors D, via Riemann's theorem.
members.name: genus
members.title: Green's conjecture

members.closest_existing_considered: Nothing in Mathlib; `FunctionField` in Mathlib.NumberTheory.FunctionField only concerns finite extensions of Fq(t) and has no genus.
members.code: noncomputable def functionFieldGenus : ℕ := Module.finrank K (regularDifferentials K L)
members.docstring:
The genus of the function field `L` over `K`: the `K`-dimension of the space of differentials
of `L/K` that are regular at every place. For `L = K(C)` the function field of a smooth
projective geometrically irreducible curve `C` over `K` this is
$\dim_K H^0(C, \Omega^1_{C/K})$, the genus of `C`.
members.meaning: The K-dimension of the space of everywhere regular differentials of L/K.
members.name: functionFieldGenus
members.title: Uniform boundedness conjecture for rational points
variables: variable (K L : Type*) [Field K] [Field L] [Algebra K L]
members.why: The representative is fixed over base field ℂ and defines genus as `sSup {deg D - ℓ(D) + 1}` (Riemann's theorem, via Riemann–Roch spaces cut out by uniformizers at places), whereas the variant is over an arbitrary base field K and defines genus as `finrank K` of the Kähler differentials regular at every valuation subring. Even after specialising K = ℂ, the two only agree for genuine one-variable function fields (a consequence of Riemann–Roch), not for arbitrary field extensions F/ℂ over which both are quantified (e.g. for ℂ(x,y) the sSup side degenerates to 0 via an unbounded set while the differential side is computed differently), so they are not the same predicate/object as defined.

groups.notes: Neither notion is in Mathlib. The two are genuinely different formal definitions: different base field generality (ℂ vs arbitrary K) and different characterisations (Riemann's max of deg D − ℓ(D) + 1 vs dim of global regular differentials); their agreement is the Riemann–Roch/duality theorem, valid only under a function-field-of-one-variable hypothesis that neither definition assumes.

groups.concept: graph embeddable in a topological space
labels: graph embeddable in a topological space

members.closest_existing_considered: Searched Mathlib and the repo for planar/toroidal/genus/embedding notions: only `SimpleGraph.Embedding` (graph homomorphisms, unrelated), `UnitDistanceEmbeddable` (metric, not topological), and `IsEmbedding` for maps (used for Jordan curves in InscribedSquare.lean, but not for graphs).
members.code:
def EmbedsIn {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (X : Type*) [TopologicalSpace X] : Prop :=
  ∃ (f : V → X) (γ : G.edgeSet → C(unitInterval, X)),
    Function.Injective f ∧
    (∀ e, Function.Injective (γ e)) ∧
    (∀ e : G.edgeSet, Sym2.map f e = s(γ e 0, γ e 1)) ∧
    (∀ (e : G.edgeSet) (v : V), f v ∈ Set.range (γ e) → v ∈ (e : Sym2 V)) ∧
    (∀ e e' : G.edgeSet, e ≠ e' → Set.range (γ e) ∩ Set.range (γ e') ⊆ Set.range f)
members.docstring:
A simple graph `G` *embeds* in a topological space `X` if there are
* an injective map `f` sending vertices to points of `X`, and
* for each edge `e`, a simple arc `γ e` in `X` (a continuous injective map from $[0,1]$)
  whose endpoints are the images of the two endpoints of `e`,

such that an arc passes through the image of a vertex only at its own endpoints, and two
distinct arcs meet only at images of vertices (hence only at common endpoints).
members.meaning: There exist an injective vertex map and injective continuous arcs for edges joining their endpoints, with arcs meeting vertex images only at endpoints and distinct arcs meeting only at vertex images.
members.name: EmbedsIn
members.title: Grünbaum–Nash-Williams conjecture

members.closest_existing_considered: Nonempty (Drawing G X) inlined; no Mathlib analogue.
members.code:
def EmbedsIn (G : SimpleGraph V) (X : Type*) [TopologicalSpace X] : Prop :=
  Nonempty (Drawing G X)
members.docstring: The simple graph `G` embeds in the topological space `X`.
members.meaning: There exists a topological embedding (drawing) of G in X.
members.name: EmbedsIn
members.title: Negami's conjecture
members.why: Both are 'injective vertex map + one simple arc per edge with matching endpoints, arcs hit vertex images only at their own endpoints, distinct arcs meet only in vertex images'. The representative indexes arcs by unoriented edges (G.edgeSet, Sym2 endpoint equation) while the variant indexes them by oriented adjacencies as Paths with a symmetry law and interior-parameter phrasing; since f u ≠ f v each arc has a unique orientation starting at f u, and the two formulations are inter-derivable (proved in the Lean check).

groups.notes: Both files formalize the standard Mohar–Thomassen notion of a topological graph embedding (vertices ↦ points, edges ↦ simple arcs meeting only at common endpoints). Neither is in Mathlib. The variant's oriented-path formulation (with edge_symm) is equivalent to the representative's unoriented edgeSet-indexed one because injectivity of the vertex map determines the orientation of each arc uniquely.

groups.concept: group embeddable in a restricted direct product of finite groups
labels: group embeddable in a restricted direct product of finite groups

members.closest_existing_considered: RestrictedProduct (Πʳ i, [F i, ⊥]) from Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.RestrictedProduct — equivalent but more exotic and topology-oriented; DFinsupp (Π₀) has only additive group structure; Function.mulSupport does not apply to dependent functions.
members.docstring:
A group $H$ is embeddable in a direct product of finite groups if there are finite groups
$F_i$, $i \in I$, and an injective homomorphism from $H$ into the Cartesian product
$\prod_{i \in I} F_i$ whose image lies in the restricted direct product $\mathrm{Dr}_{i \in I} F_i$,
that is, every element of the image has only finitely many non-trivial coordinates.
members.meaning: There is an injective homomorphism into a product of finite groups whose image elements have finite support.
members.name: IsEmbeddableInDirectProductOfFiniteGroups
members.title: Conjecture 10.17

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib's `RestrictedProduct` (`Πʳ i, [F i, (⊥ : Subgroup (F i))]`), which is used as the target; also considered the unrestricted `Π i, F i` with a `mulSupport`-finiteness condition, and `DFinsupp` (additive only).
members.docstring:
A group $H$ is *embeddable in a direct product of finite groups* if there is an
injective homomorphism from $H$ into the restricted direct product
$\mathrm{Dr}_{i \in I} F_i$ of some family $(F_i)_{i \in I}$ of finite groups, i.e. into
the subgroup of $\prod_{i \in I} F_i$ formed by the tuples with all but finitely many
coordinates equal to $1$. In Mathlib this restricted direct product is
`Πʳ i, [F i, (⊥ : Subgroup (F i))]`.
members.meaning: There is an injective homomorphism into the restricted direct product of some family of finite groups.
members.name: IsEmbeddableInDirectProductOfFiniteGroups
members.title: Conjecture 9.17
members.why: Same universe/data (ι, F : ι → Type u, Group, Finite) and same injectivity requirement; the only difference is that 9.17 targets the restricted product Πʳ i, [F i, ⊥] (a subtype of ∀ i, F i with the cofinite/finite-support condition built in) whereas 10.17 targets ∀ i, F i and states finite support of each image element separately. A hom into the subtype composed with Subtype.val gives the 10.17 data, and a finite-support hom into the product factors through the subtype, so the predicates coincide (propositionally, not definitionally).

groups.notes: Both are bespoke because Mathlib has no "embeds into a (restricted) direct product of finite groups" predicate; note that both are actually equivalent to residual finiteness (for a group, embedding into a restricted product of finite groups ⇔ embedding into a full product of finite groups ⇔ residually finite), which is also not in Mathlib.

refined to a solvable normal system of `G`.

members.name: IsRNBarGroup
members.title: Conjecture 2.22

`G` is an $\overline{SN}$-group: every normal system of `G` can be refined to a normal system
with abelian factors.
members.meaning: Every normal system is contained in a normal system with abelian factors.

members.title: Conjecture 7.41

groups.concept: group of homological type fp_∞
labels: group of homological type fp_∞

members.closest_existing_considered: `CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution` / `HasProjectiveResolution` (no finite-generation condition); `Rep.barResolution`/standard resolution (a specific, non-f.g. resolution); `Module.FinitePresentation` (only FP_1-level, for modules not groups).
members.docstring:
A group $G$ is *of type $(FP)_{\infty}$* if the trivial $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $\mathbb{Z}$
has a resolution $\cdots \to P_1 \to P_0 \to \mathbb{Z} \to 0$ by finitely generated projective
$\mathbb{Z}G$-modules $P_n$. Here a resolution is a `CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution`: a
chain complex of projective `MonoidAlgebra ℤ G`-modules together with a quasi-isomorphism to
$\mathbb{Z}$ placed in degree $0$.
members.meaning: The trivial ℤG-module has a projective resolution with all terms finitely generated.
members.name: IsTypeFPInfty
members.title: Conjecture 6.3

members.closest_existing_considered: `CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution` / `HasProjectiveResolution` (no finiteness condition), `Rep.trivial` with `Rep ℤ G` (finite generation over ℤG awkward to express there), `groupCohomology` machinery (does not encode FP_n). Built on `ProjectiveResolution` in `ModuleCat (MonoidAlgebra ℤ G)` plus `Module.Finite`.
members.code:
def IsFPInfinity (G : Type) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ P : ProjectiveResolution
      (ModuleCat.of (MonoidAlgebra ℤ G) (Representation.trivial ℤ G ℤ).asModule),
    ∀ n : ℕ, Module.Finite (MonoidAlgebra ℤ G) (P.complex.X n)
members.docstring:
A group $G$ is of type $(FP)_{\infty}$ if the trivial $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $\mathbb{Z}$ has a
projective resolution by finitely generated projective $\mathbb{Z}G$-modules, i.e. there is an
exact sequence $\cdots \to P_1 \to P_0 \to \mathbb{Z} \to 0$ of $\mathbb{Z}G$-modules with every
$P_n$ finitely generated and projective.

Here the group ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ is `MonoidAlgebra ℤ G` and the trivial module $\mathbb{Z}$ is
`(Representation.trivial ℤ G ℤ).asModule`.
members.meaning: The trivial ℤG-module ℤ has a projective resolution by finitely generated ℤG-modules.
members.name: IsFPInfinity
members.title: Conjecture 6.5
members.why: After unfolding the abbrev `trivialModule G = ModuleCat.of (MonoidAlgebra ℤ G) (Representation.trivial ℤ G ℤ).asModule`, both definitions are syntactically the same term: ∃ projective resolution of the trivial ℤG-module ℤ in ModuleCat (MonoidAlgebra ℤ G) with every term P.complex.X n a finite ℤG-module (the binder `n` is ℕ in both, explicitly or by inference).

groups.notes: Both files define FP_∞ identically: existence of a CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution of the trivial module (Representation.trivial ℤ G ℤ).asModule in ModuleCat (MonoidAlgebra ℤ G) whose every term is Module.Finite over ℤG. Only difference is that 6.3 factors the trivial module through an abbrev. Both restrict to G : Type.

The two encodings are in canonical bijection (`Fin.val`/`Fin.mk`) and under that bijection the presented groups are equal as types (the relator sets coincide), so the notion "group presented by a finite presentation" is the same; a literal textual swap is not possible only because the parameter types differ.

instance verbalSubgroup_normal (W : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) (G : Type*) [Group G] :
    (verbalSubgroup W G).Normal := by
  refine ⟨fun n hn c => ?_⟩
  refine Subgroup.closure_induction (fun x hx => ?_) ?_ (fun x y _ _ ihx ihy => ?_)
    (fun x _ ihx => ?_) hn
  · obtain ⟨w, hw, f, rfl⟩ := hx
    exact Subgroup.subset_closure ⟨w, hw, fun i => c * f i * c⁻¹, (conj_lift f c w).symm⟩
  · simp
  · rw [← conj_mul]
    exact mul_mem ihx ihy
  · rw [← conj_inv]
    exact inv_mem ihx
members.docstring:
The set of values of the words in `W` is closed under conjugation, so the verbal subgroup
`W(G)` is normal.
members.meaning: The verbal subgroup W(G) is normal since its generating set is conjugation-closed.

  exact @Subgroup.Normal.conj_smul_eq_self _ _ g N N.2.1
members.docstring: The radical is a normal subgroup, being a join of normal subgroups.
members.meaning: The 𝔛-radical of a group is a normal subgroup, being a join of normal subgroups.
members.name: radical_normal
members.title: Conjecture 8.30
members.why: Both prove normality of the same shape of join, but the underlying `radical` is defined over different ambient structures: in 3.45 `𝔛 : GroupClass.{u}` is a universe-polymorphic predicate applied directly to the subgroup type (`𝔛 N`, groups in `Type u`), whereas in 8.30 `𝔛 : Set GrpCat.{0}` is a set of bundled groups tested via `GrpCat.of N ∈ 𝔛` and `G : Type` is fixed to universe 0. The parameter types differ, so neither statement can be substituted for the other.

groups.notes: Mathematically both are the standard fact that the 𝔛-radical (join of normal 𝔛-subgroups) is normal; the difference is purely in the encoding of 'class of groups' (predicate on `Type u` vs `Set GrpCat.{0}`) and the universe restriction, which makes the two `radical` definitions and hence the two normality statements non-interchangeable. Mathlib has no general 'radical of a group class'; only `Subgroup.sup_normal` (binary) and `Subgroup.normalCore` machinery.

  normal : ∀ A ∈ 𝔄, A.Normal

An *invariant system* of `G` (Kurosh): a normal system all of whose members are normal
subgroups of `G`.
members.meaning: A normal system all of whose members are normal in G.
members.name: IsInvariantSystem
members.title: Conjecture 7.41

members.code:
structure IsInvariantSystem (𝒜 : Set (Subgroup G)) : Prop where
  normal : ∀ A ∈ 𝒜, A.Normal
  bot_mem : ⊥ ∈ 𝒜
  top_mem : ⊤ ∈ 𝒜
  isChain : IsChain (· ≤ ·) 𝒜
  sSup_mem : ∀ S ⊆ 𝒜, S.Nonempty → sSup S ∈ 𝒜
  sInf_mem : ∀ S ⊆ 𝒜, S.Nonempty → sInf S ∈ 𝒜
members.docstring:
An *invariant system* of a group $G$ (Kurosh): a set $\mathfrak{A}$ of normal subgroups
of $G$ that contains the trivial subgroup and $G$, is linearly ordered by inclusion, and is
complete, i.e. contains the union and the intersection of every nonempty subfamily.
members.meaning: A chain of normal subgroups containing ⊥ and ⊤ and closed under suprema and infima of nonempty subfamilies.
members.name: IsInvariantSystem
members.title: Conjecture 8.16
members.why: Both are 'chain of normal subgroups of G closed under sSup/sInf'. 7.41 quantifies closure over all subsets (so sSup ∅ = ⊥ and sInf ∅ = ⊤ are members), while 8.16 restricts to nonempty subsets and adds ⊥ ∈ 𝒜, ⊤ ∈ 𝒜 explicitly; 7.41's extra jump condition (A.subgroupOf B).Normal follows from A being normal in G (Subgroup.Normal.subgroupOf). Not defeq (different field structure) but logically equivalent.

groups.notes: Both files formalize Kurosh's invariant system as a complete chain of normal subgroups of G. The 7.41 version routes through IsCompleteSystem/IsNormalSystem (jump-normality is redundant once all members are normal in G); the 8.16 version is flat with explicit ⊥/⊤ membership replacing the empty-subset cases of sSup/sInf closure. Logically equivalent, not defeq.
