groups.concept: koszul differential (contraction of the exterior algebra against a linear form)
labels: koszul differential (contraction of the exterior algebra against a linear form)

members.closest_existing_considered: CliffordAlgebra.contractLeft (used), CategoryTheory.Tor (ungraded, cannot isolate β_{p,p+2}).
members.code:
noncomputable def koszulDifferential (K : Divisor F) : KoszulSpace K →ₗ[ℂ] KoszulSpace K :=
  (CliffordAlgebra.contractLeft (Q := (0 : QuadraticForm F (F ⊗[ℂ] K.riemannRochSpace)))
    (K.riemannRochSpace.subtype.liftBaseChange F)).restrictScalars ℂ
members.docstring:
The Koszul differential: contraction against the `F`-linear form
`F ⊗_ℂ 𝓛(K) → F`, `f ⊗ v ↦ f v`. On `w • (v₁ ∧ ⋯ ∧ vₙ)` it is
`∑ᵢ (-1)^(i+1) (vᵢ w) • (v₁ ∧ ⋯ ∧ v̂ᵢ ∧ ⋯ ∧ vₙ)`.
members.meaning: Contraction against the evaluation form F ⊗ L(K) → F, f ⊗ v ↦ fv, restricted to ℂ-scalars.
members.name: koszulDifferential
members.title: Green's conjecture

members.closest_existing_considered: `RingTheory.Regular.RegularSequence` only has a TODO for Koszul complexes; `HomologicalComplex` monoidal tensor products of two-term complexes were considered but give K_0 only up to iso; `Mathlib.Algebra.Homology.LocalCohomology` does not define Koszul complexes.
members.code:
noncomputable def koszulD (φ : Module.Dual R M) (n : ℕ) :
    ⋀[R]^(n + 1) M →ₗ[R] ⋀[R]^n M :=
  (CliffordAlgebra.contractLeft (Q := 0) φ).restrict (contractLeft_mem_exteriorPower φ n)
members.docstring:
The Koszul differential $\bigwedge^{n+1} M \to \bigwedge^n M$ attached to a linear form
$\varphi$ on $M$: contraction against $\varphi$, so that
$m_0 \wedge \cdots \wedge m_n \mapsto \sum_i (-1)^i \varphi(m_i)\,
m_0 \wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{m_i} \wedge \cdots \wedge m_n$.
members.meaning: The map ⋀^{n+1}M → ⋀^n M given by contraction against a linear form φ.
members.name: koszulD
members.title: Homological conjectures in commutative algebra
variables: variable {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {M : Type*} [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]
members.why: The representative is a fixed ungraded ℂ-linear endomorphism `ExteriorAlgebra F (F ⊗[ℂ] 𝓛(K)) →ₗ[ℂ] ExteriorAlgebra F (F ⊗[ℂ] 𝓛(K))` for one specific module and one specific linear form (the multiplication map), whereas `koszulD φ n` is, for an arbitrary commutative ring `R`, module `M` and dual vector `φ`, the graded component `⋀[R]^(n+1) M →ₗ[R] ⋀[R]^n M` of the contraction. Different parameters (general vs. a single specialised form), different domain/codomain (graded pieces vs. whole exterior algebra) and different scalar ring of linearity (`R` vs. `ℂ` after `restrictScalars`), so neither could replace the other in the other's statement.

groups.notes: Both are wrappers around Mathlib's `CliffordAlgebra.contractLeft` with the zero quadratic form, i.e. the same underlying interior-product operation on the exterior algebra; the difference is in what is packaged: a general graded component `⋀^{n+1} M → ⋀^n M` for arbitrary (R, M, φ) versus a single ungraded ℂ-linear endomorphism of a specific exterior algebra attached to a divisor on a function field.

groups.concept: loop (quasigroup with identity)
labels: loop (quasigroup with identity)

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib `Group`/`MulOneClass`/`IsCancelMul` — none captures non-associative loops with division operations.
members.code:
class Loop (α : Type*) extends LoopSignature α where
  one_mul : ∀ a : α, 1 * a = a
  mul_one : ∀ a : α, a * 1 = a
  mul_ldiv : ∀ a b : α, a * (a ⧵ b) = b
  ldiv_mul : ∀ a b : α, a ⧵ (a * b) = b
  rdiv_mul : ∀ a b : α, (a / b) * b = a
  mul_rdiv : ∀ a b : α, (a * b) / b = a
members.docstring:
A loop: an algebra `(L, *, ⧵, /, 1)` in the loop signature in which `1` is a two-sided
identity, `a ⧵ b` is the unique solution `x` of `a * x = b`, and `a / b` is the unique
solution `y` of `y * b = a`.
members.meaning: An algebra in the loop signature where 1 is a two-sided identity and left/right division give the unique solutions of a*x=b and y*a=b.
members.name: Loop
members.title: Conjecture 8.4

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib `MulOneClass`, `IsCancelMul`, `Group` (too strong: associative), `LatinSquare` in FormalConjecturesForMathlib (a matrix, not an algebraic structure).
members.code:
class Loop (Q : Type u) extends MulOneClass Q where
  mul_left_bijective (a : Q) : Function.Bijective (a * ·)
  mul_right_bijective (a : Q) : Function.Bijective (· * a)
members.docstring:
A *loop* is a set with a binary operation `*` and a two-sided identity `1` in which
every equation `a * x = b` and `y * a = b` has a unique solution, i.e. all left and right
translations are bijections.
members.meaning: A set with multiplication and two-sided identity in which all left and right translations are bijections.
members.name: Loop
members.title: Problems in loop theory and quasigroup theory
members.why: Both are the standard notion of a loop: a magma with two-sided identity in which all left and right translations are bijections. The Kourovka variant additionally carries the left/right division operations as data subject to the four quasigroup identities, but these identities force the divisions to be exactly the inverses of the (hence bijective) translations, so the divisions are uniquely determined; conversely from bijective translations one recovers the divisions. The two structure types are therefore in bijection (proved below as an `Equiv`), not merely mutually constructible.

groups.notes: Both variants formalize the classical notion of a loop (quasigroup with identity). Since they are data-carrying classes rather than Props, "equivalence" is checked as an `Equiv` between the structure types `Loop1 α ≃ Loop2 α`: the Kourovka variant's extra division operations are forced by its identities to be the inverse translations, so no information is added or lost. Note the two are not syntactically interchangeable as typeclass instances (one provides `Div`/`ldiv` fields, the other does not), but every statement about loops in either file transfers verbatim along this equivalence. Mathlib has no loop/quasigroup structure.

groups.concept: normal system of a group (kurosh: complete chain of subgroups with normality at jumps)
labels: normal system of a group (kurosh: complete chain of subgroups with normality at jumps)

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib `CompositionSeries` (finite length only, and requires maximality), `IsSolvable`/`derivedSeries` (finite derived series only), `IsChain`.
members.code:
structure IsNormalSystem (S : Set (Subgroup G)) : Prop where
  bot_mem : ⊥ ∈ S
  top_mem : ⊤ ∈ S
  isChain : IsChain (· ≤ ·) S
  sSup_mem : ∀ T ⊆ S, sSup T ∈ S
  sInf_mem : ∀ T ⊆ S, sInf T ∈ S

members.docstring:
A *normal system* of `G` (Kurosh; a *series* in Robinson's terminology): a set `S` of
subgroups of `G` that contains `⊥` and `⊤`, is linearly ordered by inclusion, is complete
(closed under joins and meets of arbitrary subfamilies; for a chain of subgroups the join is the
union), and in which `A` is a normal subgroup of `B` for every jump `(A, B)`. The quotients
`B ⧸ A` over the jumps are the *factors* of `S`.
members.meaning: A set of subgroups containing ⊥ and ⊤, a chain, closed under sSup and sInf of subfamilies, with A normal in B at every jump.
members.name: IsNormalSystem
members.title: Conjecture 2.22

members.closest_existing_considered: No Mathlib notion of (transfinite) normal series / serial subgroups exists; `Subgroup.Normal` and `Subgroup.subgroupOf` are used as components.

structure IsNormalSystem (𝔄 : Set (Subgroup G)) : Prop extends IsCompleteSystem 𝔄 where
  normal_of_isJump : ∀ A B, IsJump 𝔄 A B → (A.subgroupOf B).Normal
members.docstring:
A *normal system* of `G` (Kurosh): a complete system in which `A` is a normal subgroup of `B`
for every jump `(A, B)`.
members.meaning: A complete system with A normal in B for every jump (A, B).
members.name: IsNormalSystem
members.title: Conjecture 7.41
members.why: Same `IsJump` and same isChain/sSup_mem/sInf_mem/normal_of_isJump fields; the 2.22 variant additionally asks `⊥ ∈ S` and `⊤ ∈ S`, but these follow from closure under sSup/sInf applied to the empty subset (`sSup ∅ = ⊥`, `sInf ∅ = ⊤`), so the predicates are logically equivalent though not defeq (different structure fields).

groups.concept: number of crossings of a graph drawing
labels: number of crossings of a graph drawing

members.closest_existing_considered: Set.ncard / Nat.card (rejected in favour of encard for honesty on infinite graphs); a Finset sum over Sym2 pairs (needs Fintype/Decidable instances, less generic).
members.code:
noncomputable def Drawing.crossings (D : Drawing G) : ℕ∞ :=
  {x : ℝ² × Sym2 G.edgeSet | ∃ e f, e ≠ f ∧ x.2 = s(e, f) ∧
    x.1 ∈ D.arc e '' Set.Ioo 0 1 ∩ D.arc f '' Set.Ioo 0 1}.encard
members.docstring:
The number of crossings of a drawing: the number of pairs `(p, {e, f})` where `e ≠ f` are
edges and `p` is a common point of the arcs of `e` and `f` other than a shared endpoint
(equivalently, a common interior point of the two arcs). A point through which several edges pass
is thus counted once for every pair of edges through it. The count is finite whenever `G` has
finitely many edges.
members.meaning: The extended cardinality of the set of pairs (point, unordered pair of distinct edges) with the point interior to both arcs.
members.name: Drawing.crossings
members.title: Guy's conjecture on the crossing number of complete graphs

members.closest_existing_considered: No crossing-number notion exists in Mathlib or the repo (grep for 'crossing' finds only martingale upcrossings and category theory).
members.code:
noncomputable def crossings : ℕ∞ :=
  D.crossingSet.encard
members.docstring:
The number of crossings of the drawing `D`, as an element of `ℕ∞` (it is `⊤` when the
drawing has infinitely many crossings).
members.meaning: The extended cardinality of the crossing set of the drawing.
members.name: crossings
members.title: Turán's brick factory problem
members.why: The two `crossings` are defined over different ambient structures: the representative's `Drawing` has `arc : G.edgeSet → C(I, ℝ²)` and counts common *interior* points (`arc e '' Ioo 0 1`), while the variant's `Drawing` has curves indexed by adjacency proofs `h : G.Adj u v` (`D.curve h`, so `OnEdge` is an existential over orientations and `crossingSet` ranges over `Sym2 (Sym2 V)`), and counts points in the full `Set.range (D.curve h)` that are not vertex images. Since the `Drawing` types (and hence the domains of the two functions) differ and the variant's structure is not even shown (no info on whether curve endpoints are the vertices, interiors avoid vertices, or curves are orientation-independent), neither definition can replace the other.

groups.notes: Both are Set.encard : ℕ∞ of a 'point × unordered pair of distinct edges' set and are intended to count a k-fold point k.choose 2 times; under the natural assumptions on the second file's Drawing (endpoints are vertices, interiors avoid vertices, curve independent of orientation) they would be mathematically equivalent, but the second Drawing structure was not supplied and the underlying types are incomparable, so no Lean equivalence can be stated.

groups.concept: p-conjugacy biprimitively finite group (shunkov)
labels: p-conjugacy biprimitively finite group (shunkov)
p-conjugacy biprimitively finite group (for a fixed prime p)

members.closest_existing_considered: Defining it as the restriction of IsConjugacyBiprimitivelyFinite to order p; stated explicitly for readability, with an API lemma showing conjugacy ⇒ p-conjugacy for p prime.
members.code:
def IsPConjugacyBiprimitivelyFinite (p : ℕ) (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ H : Subgroup G, Finite H →
    ∀ x y : H.normalizer ⧸ H.subgroupOf H.normalizer,
      orderOf x = p → orderOf y = p → IsConj x y → Finite (Subgroup.closure {x, y})
members.docstring:
A group $G$ is *$p$-conjugacy biprimitively finite* if for every finite subgroup
$H \le G$, any two conjugate elements of order $p$ in $N_G(H)/H$ generate a finite
subgroup.
members.meaning: For every finite subgroup H, any two conjugate elements of order exactly p in N_G(H)/H generate a finite subgroup.
members.name: IsPConjugacyBiprimitivelyFinite
members.title: Conjecture 6.62

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib has `Monoid.IsTorsion`, `IsPGroup`, `Sylow`, `IsConj`, `Subgroup.normalizer` and `Subgroup.normal_in_normalizer` (used as building blocks), but no notion of (conjugately/p-conjugacy) biprimitively finite / Shunkov groups; `rg` for 'shunkov', 'biprimitiv', 'conjugately' in the repo and Mathlib found nothing.
members.code:
def IsPConjugacyBiprimitivelyFinite (p : ℕ) (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ H : Subgroup G, Finite H →
    ∀ x y : H.normalizer ⧸ H.subgroupOf H.normalizer,
      orderOf x = p → orderOf y = p → IsConj x y → Finite (Subgroup.closure {x, y})
members.docstring:
A group $G$ is *$p$-conjugacy biprimitively finite* (V. P. Shunkov, Kourovka Notebook
Problem 6.59) if for every finite subgroup $H$ of $G$, any two conjugate elements of order
$p$ in the quotient $N_G(H)/H$ generate a finite subgroup.
members.meaning: For every finite subgroup H, any two conjugate elements of order p in N_G(H)/H generate a finite subgroup.
members.name: IsPConjugacyBiprimitivelyFinite
members.title: Conjecture 9.83
members.why: The definition bodies are textually identical: same quantification over finite subgroups H, same quotient N_G(H)/H (as H.normalizer ⧸ H.subgroupOf H.normalizer), same orderOf = p and IsConj hypotheses, same conclusion Finite (Subgroup.closure {x, y}); both bind p, G and [Group G] explicitly in the def.

groups.notes: Two verbatim copies of the same definition (Shunkov's p-conjugacy biprimitively finite groups, Kourovka 6.59); no Mathlib counterpart exists.

groups.concept: parallelohedron (convex polytope tiling space by translations)
labels: parallelohedron (convex polytope tiling space by translations)

members.closest_existing_considered: None; built from `convexHull`, `interior`, and `TilesByTranslation`.
members.docstring:
A *parallelohedron*: a convex polyhedron in `ℝ³` (the convex hull of a finite set, with
nonempty interior) that tiles space by translation. By the theorems of Fedorov, Minkowski,
Venkov and McMullen these are precisely the parallelepipeds, hexagonal prisms, rhombic
dodecahedra, elongated dodecahedra and truncated octahedra (up to combinatorial equivalence),
and every such convex polyhedron also tiles space face-to-face by a lattice of translations.
members.meaning: Convex hull of a finite set with nonempty interior that tiles space by translates.
members.name: IsParallelohedron
members.title: Grünbaum's conjecture on spherical polyhedra that tile space by translation

members.closest_existing_considered: `convexHull ℝ (S : Finset _)` with `(interior _).Nonempty`, as used in FormalConjectures/Paper/Rupert.lean; used as the building block.
members.code:
def IsParallelohedron (P : Set (ℝ^d)) : Prop :=
  (∃ S : Finset (ℝ^d), P = convexHull ℝ ↑S) ∧ (interior P).Nonempty ∧ TilesByTranslations P
members.docstring:
A *parallelohedron* in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a $d$-dimensional convex polytope, i.e. the convex hull
of a finite set of points with nonempty interior, that tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ by translations.
The nonempty interior condition expresses that the polytope is genuinely $d$-dimensional.
members.meaning: Convex hull of a finite set with nonempty interior tiling ℝ^d by translations.
members.name: IsParallelohedron
members.title: In parallelohedron: the Voronoi conjecture
members.why: Same three conjuncts (finite convex hull, nonempty interior, tiling by translates with pairwise disjoint interiors via an identical TilesByTranslation(s) definition), but the ambient space differs: the representative is fixed to ℝ³, while the variant is over ℝ^d for arbitrary d : ℕ. The variant is a strict generalization (a family of predicates indexed by d), so the representative cannot replace it in statements about general d; they coincide only in the special case d = 3 (and even then only if the local notations ℝ³ and ℝ^3 denote the same type, e.g. EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)).

groups.notes: Both variants are literally the same formula modulo ambient space; the only difference is dimension 3 vs general d. If the downstream use is restricted to d = 3 and the notations ℝ³ / ℝ^d unfold to EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin _), the two are definitionally equal at d = 3 (`Iff.rfl`).

groups.concept: petersen graph (as kneser graph kg(5,2))
labels: petersen graph (as kneser graph kg(5,2))

members.closest_existing_considered: WrittenOnTheWallII.Test.PetersenGraph (test-file abbrev, not reusable); no Kneser graph in Mathlib (searched `rg -i kneser`).
members.code:
def petersenGraph : SimpleGraph {s : Finset (Fin 5) // s.card = 2} where
  Adj s t := Disjoint s.1 t.1
  symm _ _ h := h.symm
  loopless s h := by
    have hs := s.2
    simp only [Finset.disjoint_self_iff_empty] at h
    simp [h] at hs
members.docstring:
The Petersen graph, realised as the Kneser graph $KG(5, 2)$: its vertices are the $10$
two-element subsets of a five-element set, and two of them are adjacent if and only if they are
disjoint.
members.meaning: The graph on 2-subsets of Fin 5 with adjacency given by disjointness.
members.name: petersenGraph
members.title: Jaeger's Petersen-coloring conjecture

members.closest_existing_considered: `PetersenGraph` in FormalConjectures/WrittenOnTheWallII/Test.lean (explicit edge list on Fin 10); Mathlib has no Kneser or Petersen graph.
members.code:
def petersenGraph : SimpleGraph {s : Finset (Fin 5) // s.card = 2} where
  Adj s t := Disjoint s.1 t.1
  symm _ _ h := h.symm
  loopless s h := by
    have hs := s.2
    simp only [disjoint_self, Finset.bot_eq_empty] at h
    simp [h] at hs
members.docstring:
The Petersen graph, realised as the Kneser graph `KG(5,2)`: the vertices are the 2-element
subsets of a 5-element set, and two vertices are adjacent when the subsets are disjoint.
members.meaning: The graph on 2-subsets of Fin 5 with adjacency given by disjointness.
members.name: petersenGraph
members.title: Petersen graph: Tutte's 4-flow conjecture
members.why: Same vertex type {s : Finset (Fin 5) // s.card = 2} and same Adj := Disjoint s.1 t.1; only the (Prop-valued) loopless proof script differs, which is irrelevant by proof irrelevance, so the two graphs are definitionally equal via rfl.

groups.notes: Both files define the Petersen graph as KG(5,2) on 2-subsets of Fin 5 with adjacency = disjointness; the definitions coincide exactly (only proof terms differ). Mathlib has no Petersen/Kneser graph, so a shared definition would be appropriate.

groups.concept: pro-p group (all finite continuous quotients are p-groups)
labels: pro-p group (all finite continuous quotients are p-groups)

members.closest_existing_considered: `ProfiniteGrp`, `IsPGroup` (used as building blocks); searched Mathlib and FormalConjecturesForMathlib for pro-p / IsProP — nothing.
members.code:
def IsProP (p : ℕ) (G : ProfiniteGrp.{u}) : Prop :=
  ∀ U : OpenNormalSubgroup G, IsPGroup p (G ⧸ U.toSubgroup)
members.docstring:
A profinite group $G$ is a pro-$p$ group if every finite continuous quotient $G/U$, for
$U$ an open normal subgroup of $G$, is a $p$-group. Equivalently, $G$ is an inverse limit of
finite $p$-groups.
members.meaning: For every open normal subgroup U of the profinite group, G/U is a p-group.
members.name: IsProP
members.title: Conjecture 5.27

members.closest_existing_considered: IsPGroup p G on the abstract group (wrong: e.g. ℤ_p is pro-p but not a p-group abstractly); used instead on the finite quotients G ⧸ N.
members.code:
def IsProP (p : ℕ) (G : ProfiniteGrp.{u}) : Prop :=
  ∀ N : OpenNormalSubgroup G, IsPGroup p (G ⧸ N.toSubgroup)
members.docstring:
A profinite group $G$ is a *pro-$p$ group* if all of its finite continuous quotients are
$p$-groups, i.e. $G / N$ is a $p$-group for every open normal subgroup $N$ of $G$. Equivalently,
$G$ is an inverse limit of finite $p$-groups.
members.meaning: G/N is a p-group for every open normal subgroup N.
members.name: IsProP
members.title: Conjecture 7.38
members.why: Same statement: for every open normal subgroup of the profinite group G, the quotient is a p-group (IsPGroup); only the bound variable name differs (U vs N).

groups.notes: Both variants define pro-p as: every quotient by an open normal subgroup is a p-group. Identical up to bound-variable name.

labels: quasivariety of groups

def IsQuasivariety (𝒦 : GroupClass) : Prop :=
  ∃ Q : Set QuasiIdentity, ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], 𝒦 G ↔ ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Holds G
members.docstring:
A class of groups is a *quasivariety* if it consists exactly of the groups in which every
quasi-identity from some set `Q` of quasi-identities holds.
members.meaning: A class of groups that is exactly the class of models of some set of quasi-identities.
members.name: IsQuasivariety
members.title: Conjecture 8.55

members.closest_existing_considered: Filter.Product / FirstOrder.Language.Ultraproduct (only a first-order Structure on ultraproducts, no Group instance for dependent families of groups), hence the syntactic definition instead.
members.docstring:
A class `𝔎` of groups is a *quasivariety* if it consists exactly of the groups
satisfying some set `Q` of quasi-identities.
members.meaning: A class of groups that is exactly the class of groups satisfying some set of quasi-identities.
members.name: IsQuasivariety
members.title: Conjecture 9.5
members.why: Both say: ∃ a set Q of quasi-identities (same structure: Finset of premise words in FreeGroup ℕ plus one conclusion word) such that 𝒦 G ↔ every q ∈ Q holds in G, with 'holds' defined verbatim the same way (argument order G/q and binder names differ only cosmetically). The only distinction is that 9.5 is universe-polymorphic (Type u) while 8.55 is fixed at Type; at u = 0 the two definitions are syntactically the same and the check is by Iff.rfl.

groups.notes: The two definitions coincide exactly at universe 0. Caveat: kourovka-9.5's version is universe-polymorphic (classes of groups in Type u), whereas kourovka-8.55's is fixed to carriers in Type; substituting 8.55's definition into a 9.5 statement at a nonzero universe would not typecheck. Neither notion (quasivariety / quasi-identity of groups) exists in Mathlib.

  ((singularHomologyFunctor (ModuleCat ℚ) n).obj (ModuleCat.of ℚ ℚ)).obj (TopCat.of X)
members.docstring:
The `n`-th rational singular homology group $H_n(X; \mathbb{Q})$ of a topological
space `X`, as a `ℚ`-module.
members.meaning: H_n(X; ℚ) as an object of ModuleCat ℚ via the singular homology functor.
members.name: rationalHomology

members.closest_existing_considered: AlgebraicTopology.singularHomologyFunctor (used directly as the building block).
members.code:
noncomputable abbrev rationalHomology (X : Type u) [TopologicalSpace X] (k : ℕ) :
    ModuleCat.{u} ℚ :=
  ((singularHomologyFunctor (ModuleCat.{u} ℚ) k).obj (ModuleCat.of ℚ (ULift.{u} ℚ))).obj
    (TopCat.of X)
members.docstring:
The `k`-th singular homology group of the topological space `X` with rational coefficients,
as a `ℚ`-module.
members.meaning: k-th singular homology of X with (ULift) ℚ coefficients as a ℚ-module.
members.name: rationalHomology
members.title: Hopf conjecture
members.why: The variant is universe-polymorphic (X : Type u, values in ModuleCat.{u} ℚ) with coefficient module ULift.{u} ℚ, whereas the representative is fixed to X : Type with coefficient module ℚ; the representative cannot be applied to spaces in Type u for u ≠ 0, and even at u = 0 the coefficient objects ℚ and ULift ℚ are distinct types, so the resulting homology objects are only canonically isomorphic, not equal.

groups.notes: Both are specializations of Mathlib's AlgebraicTopology.singularHomologyFunctor to rational coefficients and agree mathematically (canonically isomorphic ℚ-modules H_n(X;ℚ)). The 'different' verdict reflects universe of quantification (Type vs Type u) and coefficient object (ℚ vs ULift ℚ), which prevent literal interchangeability / equality as objects of ModuleCat ℚ. Any statement depending only on the isomorphism class (e.g. dimension/Betti numbers) would be unaffected.

groups.concept: relation rank: minimal number of defining relators of a group on a minimal generating set
labels: relation rank: minimal number of defining relators of a group on a minimal generating set

members.closest_existing_considered: PresentedGroup, Group.rank, Subgroup.normalClosure (used as building blocks); no Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib notion of relation rank / deficiency exists.
members.docstring:
$r_1(G)$: the minimal number of defining relations of a finitely generated group $G$ on
$d = d(G)$ generators, where $d(G)$ is the minimal number of generators of $G$ (`Group.rank G`).
That is, the least $n$ such that $G \cong F_d / \langle\langle S \rangle\rangle$ for a set $S$ of
$n$ elements of the free (discrete) group $F_d$ on $d$ generators.

When $G$ is finite such a finite presentation always exists, so the infimum is attained.
members.meaning: The least n such that G is presented on Group.rank G generators by n relators (in ℕ via sInf).
members.name: discreteRelationRank
members.title: Conjecture 5.26

members.closest_existing_considered: None; built on the bespoke relationRank and IsBasis.
members.code:
noncomputable def minRelationRank (G : Type*) [Group G] [Group.FG G] : ℕ∞ :=
  ⨅ (M : Finset G) (_ : IsBasis M), relationRank M
members.docstring:
The number $r(G)$: the minimum of $r_M(G)$ over all bases $M$ of the finitely generated group
$G$.
members.meaning: The ℕ∞-minimum over all bases M of the relation rank on M.
members.name: minRelationRank
members.title: Conjecture 7.57
members.why: Codomain ℕ vs ℕ∞: for a finitely generated but not finitely presented group the representative returns sInf ∅ = 0 while the variant returns ⊤; also the variant quantifies over bases M ⊆ G with the canonical map FreeGroup M → G whereas the representative allows an arbitrary isomorphism PresentedGroup S ≃* G on Fin (rank G) (these two agree mathematically, but the ℕ/ℕ∞ discrepancy makes the notions non-interchangeable). They coincide (under the coercion ℕ → ℕ∞) exactly when G is finitely presented, e.g. for all finite G.

groups.notes: Both are the classical r(G) = min over minimal generating sets of the number of relators; the only real difference is the treatment of non-finitely-presented f.g. groups (0 vs ⊤) and the codomain type. For finite groups (the setting of Kourovka 5.26) the values agree under coercion.

labels: relatively free group of the variety defined by a set of laws (f_x / w(f_x))

abbrev RelativelyFreeGroup (W : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) (n : ℕ) : Type :=
  FreeGroup (Fin n) ⧸ verbalSubgroup W (FreeGroup (Fin n))
members.docstring:
The free group of rank `n` in the variety of groups defined by the set of laws `W`, i.e.
the relatively free group `Fₙ / W(Fₙ)`, the quotient of the (absolutely) free group `Fₙ` of
rank `n` by its verbal subgroup.
members.meaning: The quotient of the free group on Fin n by its verbal subgroup for W.
members.name: RelativelyFreeGroup
members.title: Conjecture 4.11

members.closest_existing_considered: FreeGroup, QuotientGroup (no relatively free group in Mathlib).
members.code:
abbrev RelativelyFreeGroup (W : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) (X : Type*) : Type _ :=
  FreeGroup X ⧸ verbalSubgroup W (FreeGroup X)
members.docstring:
The (relatively) free group of the variety $\mathfrak{V}(W)$ on the set `X` of free
generators, namely $F_X / W(F_X)$ where $F_X$ is the (absolutely) free group on `X`.
members.meaning: The quotient of the free group on X by its verbal subgroup for W.
members.name: RelativelyFreeGroup
members.title: Conjecture 4.72
members.why: The 4.72 variant is parametrised by an arbitrary generating type `X : Type*` (any rank, possibly infinite), whereas the 4.11 variant only takes a finite rank `n : ℕ` with generators `Fin n`; so 4.11 cannot replace 4.72 in a statement quantifying over arbitrary `X`. (Additionally 4.11 quotients by `Subgroup.closure` and 4.72 by `Subgroup.normalClosure` of the same value set; these subgroups are provably equal since the value set is conjugation-closed, so on `X = Fin n` the two groups agree up to a propositional subgroup equality, but not definitionally.)

groups.notes: Neither relatively free groups nor verbal subgroups exist in Mathlib. The 4.72 definition strictly generalises the 4.11 one: instantiating X := Fin n recovers 4.11 modulo the (provable) equality Subgroup.closure S = Subgroup.normalClosure S for the conjugation-closed value set S.

members.docstring:
The *representation number* of a graph `G` is the least `k` such that `G` is

members.why: Different codomain and different value on non-word-representable graphs: the representative is ℕ-valued via sInf (equal to 0 when no k works), whereas this variant is ℕ∞-valued via ⨅ (equal to ⊤ when no k works). The underlying sets {k | IsKRepresentable G k} agree (the dependencies Alternate/Represents/IsKRepresentable are equivalent up to argument order and Iff direction), so the two agree as ℕ∞ after coercion exactly on word-representable graphs, but not in general and not as terms of the same type.

groups.notes: The dependency chain is equivalent between the two files: Alternate is syntactically identical, IsRepresentedBy G w ↔ Represents w G (only Iff direction and argument order differ), and the two IsKRepresentable differ only by conjunct order. Only the top-level invariant differs (ℕ with sInf/0-default vs ℕ∞ with ⨅/⊤-default). For word-representable graphs (e.g. all bipartite graphs, as the first file's docstring notes) the values agree after coercion ℕ → ℕ∞, but as definitions they are not interchangeable.

noncomputable def riemann (x₀ : M) (y : E) (u v w : E) : E :=
  fderiv ℝ (fun z ↦ christoffel I x₀ z v w) y u - fderiv ℝ (fun z ↦ christoffel I x₀ z u w) y v
    + christoffel I x₀ y u (christoffel I x₀ y v w) - christoffel I x₀ y v (christoffel I x₀ y u w)

`extChartAt I x₀`, for coordinate vector fields `u`, `v`, `w` (which commute):
`R(u, v) w = ∂ᵤ Γ(v, w) - ∂ᵥ Γ(u, w) + Γ(u, Γ(v, w)) - Γ(v, Γ(u, w))`.

These agree on the interior of the chart target for boundaryless models but not as functions of `y : E` in general. The ambient structures also differ: the representative assumes `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [EMetricSpace M]` and no `IsManifold`, while the variant assumes `[TopologicalSpace M] [IsManifold I 1 M]` (needed for the tangent-bundle trivialization) and no finite-dimensionality, so neither can be substituted for the other in the other file's context.

noncomputable def metricInChart (p : M) (y : E) : E →L[ℝ] E →L[ℝ] ℝ :=
  (innerSL ℝ (E := TangentSpace I ((extChartAt I p).symm y))).bilinearComp
    ((trivializationAt E (TangentSpace I) p).symmL ℝ ((extChartAt I p).symm y))
    ((trivializationAt E (TangentSpace I) p).symmL ℝ ((extChartAt I p).symm y))
members.docstring:
The Riemannian metric of `M` written in the chart at `p`: for `y` in the target of
`extChartAt I p`, this is the bilinear form on `E` obtained by pulling back the inner product on
the tangent space at `(extChartAt I p).symm y` along the trivialization of the tangent bundle
associated with the chart at `p`. In other words, `metricInChart I p y u v` is the value on the
coordinate vectors `u`, `v` of the metric coefficients at the chart coordinate `y`.
members.meaning: Pullback of the tangent-space inner product at the chart preimage of y along the tangent bundle trivialisation at p, as a bilinear form on E.

variables:
variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  {H : Type*} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H)
  {M : Type*} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M] [IsManifold I 1 M]
  [RiemannianBundle (fun x : M ↦ TangentSpace I x)]
members.why: metricCoord pulls the fibre inner product back along `mfderiv 𝓘(ℝ,E) I (extChartAt I x₀).symm y` (which is `fderiv` of `extChartAt I x ∘ (extChartAt I x₀).symm`, and is the junk value 0 wherever the inverse chart is not `MDifferentiableAt`), whereas metricInChart pulls it back along `(trivializationAt E (TangentSpace I) p).symmL ℝ x`, i.e. the tangent-bundle core coordinate change `fderivWithin ℝ (…) (range I) y` (junk value 0 when `x` leaves the chart's source). These agree only at interior points of the chart target on a `C¹` manifold; they differ at boundary points of `range I` (fderivWithin on `range I` vs. fderiv/0), for `y` outside `(extChartAt I p).target`, and metricCoord's context has no `IsManifold I 1 M` (so the mfderiv can be 0 everywhere) and additionally assumes `EMetricSpace M` and `FiniteDimensional ℝ E`.

groups.notes: Both are 'metric coefficients in a chart' pulled back from the RiemannianBundle inner product on TangentSpace, but via different coordinate maps (mfderiv of the inverse chart vs Trivialization.symmL of the tangent bundle), which coincide only on the interior of the chart target of a C¹ manifold; the ambient hypotheses also differ (EMetricSpace M + FiniteDimensional E vs TopologicalSpace M + IsManifold I 1 M).

members.code:
noncomputable def sectionalCurvature (x₀ : M) (u v : E) : ℝ :=
  let y := extChartAt I x₀ x₀
  let g := metricCoord I x₀ y
  g (riemann I x₀ y u v v) u / (g u u * g v v - (g u v) ^ 2)
members.docstring:
The sectional curvature of `M` at `x₀` along the plane spanned by the tangent vectors with
coordinates `u` and `v` in the chart `extChartAt I x₀`:
$$K(u, v) = \frac{g(R(u, v) v, u)}{g(u, u) g(v, v) - g(u, v)^2}.$$
It is only meaningful when `u` and `v` are linearly independent. With these conventions the
round sphere has `K = 1` and hyperbolic space has `K = -1`.
members.meaning: K(u,v)=g(R(u,v)v,u)/(g(u,u)g(v,v)−g(u,v)²) computed in the chart at x₀, meaningful for linearly independent u,v.

groups.concept: selberg class
labels: selberg class

members.closest_existing_considered: `LSeries`, `LSeriesHasSum`, `DirichletCharacter.LFunction`, `riemannZeta`, `ArithmeticFunction.IsMultiplicative`, `HasProd`/`eulerProduct` — all specific objects or building blocks, no axiomatic class.
members.code:
structure SelbergClass where
  /-- The Dirichlet coefficients $a_n$. -/
  coeff : ℕ → ℂ
  /-- The meromorphic continuation $F(s)$ of the Dirichlet series to the complex plane. -/
  toFun : ℂ → ℂ
  /-- For $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$, the Dirichlet series $\sum_{n \ge 1} a_n n^{-s}$ converges
  to $F(s)$. -/
  lSeriesHasSum : ∀ s : ℂ, 1 < s.re → LSeriesHasSum coeff s (toFun s)
  /-- **Analyticity**: for some integer $m \ge 0$, the function $(s - 1)^m F(s)$ agrees away from
  $s = 1$ with an entire function $G$ of finite order, i.e. $|G(s)| \le C \exp(|s|^\rho)$ for
  some constants $C, \rho$. In particular $F$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb{C}$ with its only
  possible pole at $s = 1$. -/
  analyticity : ∃ (m : ℕ) (G : ℂ → ℂ), Differentiable ℂ G ∧
    (∃ C ρ : ℝ, ∀ s, ‖G s‖ ≤ C * Real.exp (‖s‖ ^ ρ)) ∧
    ∀ s, s ≠ 1 → G s = (s - 1) ^ m * toFun s
  /-- **Ramanujan conjecture**, first part: $a_1 = 1$. -/
  coeff_one : coeff 1 = 1
  /-- **Ramanujan conjecture**, second part: $a_n \ll_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon$ for every
  $\varepsilon > 0$. -/
  coeff_isBigO : ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → coeff =O[atTop] fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ) ^ ε
  /-- The gamma factor $\gamma(s) = Q^s \prod_{i=1}^{k} \Gamma(\omega_i s + \mu_i)$. -/
  gamma : GammaFactor
  /-- The root number $\alpha$. -/
  rootNumber : ℂ
  /-- The root number satisfies $|\alpha| = 1$. -/
  norm_rootNumber : ‖rootNumber‖ = 1
  /-- **Functional equation**: $\Phi(s) = \alpha\,\overline{\Phi(1 - \overline{s})}$, where
  $\Phi(s) = \gamma(s) F(s)$. The identity is required at every $s$ where both sides are free of
  poles: $s \ne 0$, $s \ne 1$, and neither $s$ nor $1 - \overline{s}$ is a pole of $\gamma$. -/
  functionalEquation : ∀ s : ℂ, s ≠ 0 → s ≠ 1 →
    ¬ gamma.IsPole s → ¬ gamma.IsPole (1 - conj s) →
      gamma.toFun s * toFun s = rootNumber * conj (gamma.toFun (1 - conj s) * toFun (1 - conj s))
  /-- **Euler product**: there are coefficients $b_{p^n}$ with $b_{p^n} = O(p^{n\theta})$
  (uniformly in the prime $p$ and $n \ge 1$) for some $\theta < 1/2$, such that for
  $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$,
  $$F(s) = \prod_p F_p(s), \qquad F_p(s) = \exp\Big(\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{b_{p^n}}{p^{ns}}\Big).$$ -/
  eulerProduct : ∃ b : ℕ → ℂ,
    (∃ θ : ℝ, θ < 1 / 2 ∧ ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ p n : ℕ, p.Prime → 1 ≤ n →
      ‖b (p ^ n)‖ ≤ C * (p : ℝ) ^ (n * θ)) ∧
    ∀ s : ℂ, 1 < s.re →
      HasProd (fun p : Nat.Primes =>
        exp (∑' n : ℕ, b (p ^ (n + 1)) / ((p : ℕ) : ℂ) ^ (((n : ℂ) + 1) * s))) (toFun s)
members.docstring:
An element of the **Selberg class**: a Dirichlet series $F(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} a_n n^{-s}$,
given by its coefficients `coeff` and its meromorphic continuation `toFun`, together with a gamma
factor `gamma` and a root number `rootNumber`, satisfying Selberg's axioms (analyticity, Ramanujan
conjecture, functional equation, Euler product).

Since Lean functions `ℂ → ℂ` cannot take the value $\infty$, the continuation `toFun` is only
constrained away from $s = 1$; its value at $s = 1$ is irrelevant. Likewise, the functional
equation is only required at points where neither side involves a pole, which determines the
identity of meromorphic functions by the identity theorem.
members.meaning: A Dirichlet series with its meromorphic continuation, gamma factor and root number satisfying Selberg's axioms (analyticity of finite order, Ramanujan bound, functional equation, Euler product with θ < 1/2).
members.name: SelbergClass
members.title: Generalized Riemann hypothesis for the Selberg class

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib's LSeries, LSeriesHasSum, ArithmeticFunction (used as building blocks); ZMod.LFunction / DirichletCharacter.LFunction (only specific L-functions, not an axiomatic class); NumberField.dedekindZeta (naive LSeries, no continuation).
members.code:
def selbergClass : Set (ArithmeticFunction ℂ) :=
  {a | a 1 = 1 ∧
    (∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → (fun n : ℕ => a n) =O[atTop] fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ) ^ ε) ∧
    ∃ F : ℂ → ℂ,
      (∀ s : ℂ, 1 < s.re → LSeriesHasSum a s (F s)) ∧
      (∃ (m : ℕ) (G : ℂ → ℂ), IsEntireOfFiniteOrder G ∧
        ∀ s : ℂ, s ≠ 1 → G s = (s - 1) ^ m * F s) ∧
      (∃ (Q : ℝ) (d : ℕ) (α : Fin d → ℝ) (r : Fin d → ℂ) (w : ℂ),
        0 < Q ∧ (∀ i, 0 < α i) ∧ (∀ i, 0 ≤ (r i).re) ∧ ‖w‖ = 1 ∧
        ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 →
          (Q : ℂ) ^ s * (∏ i, Gamma (α i * s + r i)) * F s =
            w * conj ((Q : ℂ) ^ (1 - conj s) * (∏ i, Gamma (α i * (1 - conj s) + r i)) *
              F (1 - conj s))) ∧
      (∃ (b : ℕ → ℂ) (θ : ℝ), θ < 1 / 2 ∧
        (∃ C : ℝ, ∀ p k : ℕ, p.Prime → 0 < k → ‖b (p ^ k)‖ ≤ C * (p : ℝ) ^ (k * θ)) ∧
        ∀ s : ℂ, 1 < s.re →
          HasProd (fun p : Nat.Primes => exp (∑' k : ℕ, b (p ^ (k + 1)) / (p : ℂ) ^ ((k + 1) * s)))
            (F s))}
members.docstring:
The **Selberg class** $\mathcal{S}$, as a set of coefficient sequences
`a : ArithmeticFunction ℂ`.
The sequence `a` belongs to `selbergClass` if the Dirichlet series
$F(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} a_n n^{-s}$ satisfies Selberg's axioms:

1. (Dirichlet series) $a_1 = 1$ and the series converges absolutely for $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1$.
2. (Analytic continuation) $F$ extends to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ such that
   $(s - 1)^m F(s)$ is an entire function of finite order for some integer $m \ge 0$.
3. (Functional equation) There are $Q > 0$, $\alpha_i > 0$, $\operatorname{Re}(r_i) \ge 0$
   ($1 \le i \le d$) and $w \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|w| = 1$ such that
   $\Phi(s) = Q^s \prod_{i=1}^d \Gamma(\alpha_i s + r_i) F(s)$ satisfies
   $\Phi(s) = w \overline{\Phi(1 - \overline{s})}$.
4. (Euler product) $F(s) = \prod_p F_p(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1$, where
   $F_p(s) = \exp\left(\sum_{k \ge 1} b_{p^k} p^{-ks}\right)$ and $b_{p^k} = O(p^{k\theta})$
   for some $\theta < 1/2$.
5. (Ramanujan hypothesis) $a_n = O(n^\varepsilon)$ for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$.

The continuation `F` is only used at points `s ≠ 1`, so its value at the possible pole `s = 1`
is irrelevant. The functional equation is required on the strip $0 < \operatorname{Re}(s) < 1$,
which is mapped to itself by $s \mapsto 1 - \overline{s}$ and contains no pole of $F$ or of the
gamma factors. Both sides are meromorphic on $\mathbb{C}$, so by the identity theorem this is
equivalent to the functional equation as an identity of meromorphic functions.
members.meaning: Set of coefficient sequences a with a_1 = 1, Ramanujan bound, a continuation F with (s−1)^m F entire of finite order, a gamma-factor functional equation on the critical strip, and an Euler product with θ < 1/2.
members.name: selbergClass
members.title: Selberg's orthogonality conjecture
members.why: Mathematically both encode Selberg's axioms for the same class, and `a ∈ selbergClass ↔ ∃ S : SelbergClass, ⇑S.coeff = ⇑a` should hold, but the formalizations differ in kind and content: the representative is a Type bundling non-unique data (continuation, gamma factor, root number) while the variant is a Set of ArithmeticFunctions with all of that existential (and requires a 0 = 0); the finite-order bound is `C·exp(‖s‖^ρ)` vs `A·exp(B·‖s‖^ρ)`; and the functional equation is demanded at every non-pole point s ≠ 0,1 (incl. Re s > 1 and Re s < 0) vs only on the strip 0 < Re s < 1. The strip version implies the full version only via the identity theorem for meromorphic functions (using the other axioms), so the equivalence is a genuine theorem, not a syntactic/defeq match, and I cannot supply a verified Lean proof.

groups.notes: Neither notion exists in Mathlib. The two files agree on the informal Selberg class, but one formalizes it as a bundled structure (Type, with gamma factor/root number as data) and the other as a Set of coefficient sequences. Easy direction: a `SelbergClass` term yields membership of its `coeff` in `selbergClass` (the strip 0<Re s<1 avoids 0, 1 and all gamma poles since ω_i>0, Re μ_i≥0; take B = 1 in the finite-order bound). Hard direction (membership → structure) needs the identity theorem to extend the functional equation from the strip to all non-pole points, plus a compactness argument to remove the constant B from the finite-order bound. A human should decide whether this counts as 'equivalent' for their purposes.

  ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], SetHolds S G → q.Holds G
members.docstring:
The quasiidentity `q` is a consequence of the set `S` of quasiidentities (modulo the group
axioms): every group satisfying `S` satisfies `q`.
members.meaning: q follows from S if every group (in Type) satisfying S satisfies q.
members.name: Follows
members.title: Conjecture 8.64

members.closest_existing_considered: `FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ModelsBoundedFormula` (`⊨ᵇ`), not usable without a group language.
members.code:
def IsConsequence (B : Set QuasiIdentity) (q : QuasiIdentity) : Prop :=
  ∀ (H : Type) [Group H], (∀ p ∈ B, p.Holds H) → q.Holds H
members.docstring:
The quasi-identity `q` is a consequence of the set `B` of quasi-identities: every group in
which all members of `B` hold is a group in which `q` holds.
members.meaning: Every group (in Type) satisfying all members of B satisfies q.
members.name: IsConsequence
members.title: Conjecture 9.6
members.why: The consequence relation itself has the identical form (∀ (G : Type) [Group G], (∀ p ∈ S, p.Holds G) → q.Holds G, with SetHolds unfolding to the inner ∀), but it is a predicate on a different type of syntactic object: 8.64's Quasiidentity has a fixed variable count `numVars` with words in `FreeGroup (Fin numVars)` and a `List` of premises evaluated at `x : Fin n → G`, whereas 9.6's QuasiIdentity uses words in `FreeGroup ℕ`, a `Finset` of premises and assignments `x : ℕ → H`. Since `Set Quasiidentity` and `Set QuasiIdentity` are unrelated types, neither definition can replace the other in the other file's statement; they agree only up to a non-trivial translation (Fin n ↪ ℕ, List ↦ Finset) that is not part of either definition.

groups.notes: Both files define semantic consequence modulo the group axioms in the same way (quantifying over all groups in `Type`), so mathematically they are the 'same' meta-notion; the difference lies entirely in the encoding of quasi-identities (Fin-indexed variables + List premises vs ℕ-indexed variables + Finset premises). These encodings are equi-expressive (a Fin-n quasi-identity embeds into the ℕ one, and every ℕ one uses finitely many variables), but the Lean types are distinct so the definitions are not interchangeable. Neither is in Mathlib; Mathlib's `FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ModelsBoundedFormula` would be the natural home but there is no group language there.

groups.concept: serre intersection multiplicity χ(m, n)
labels: serre intersection multiplicity χ(m, n)

members.closest_existing_considered: `CategoryTheory.Tor` and `Module.length` exist and are used; no intersection multiplicity in Mathlib.
members.code:
noncomputable def serreMultiplicity (d : ℕ) (M N : Type u) [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]
    [AddCommGroup N] [Module R N] : ℤ :=
  ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (d + 1), (-1 : ℤ) ^ i *
    ((Module.length R (((Tor (ModuleCat.{u} R) i).obj (ModuleCat.of R M)).obj
      (ModuleCat.of R N))).toNat : ℤ)
members.docstring:
Serre's intersection multiplicity
$$\chi(M, N) = \sum_{i = 0}^{d} (-1)^i \,\ell\bigl(\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M, N)\bigr)$$
of two finitely generated modules $M$, $N$ over a regular local ring $R$ of dimension $d$. Over
such a ring $\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M, N) = 0$ for $i > d$, so this is the full alternating sum,
and when $M \otimes_R N$ has finite length so does every $\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M, N)$, so
that the conversion `ENat.toNat` of the lengths is lossless.
members.meaning: Σ_{i=0}^d (−1)^i ℓ(Tor_i^R(M, N)), truncated at the dimension d.
members.name: serreMultiplicity
members.title: Homological conjectures in commutative algebra
variables: variable {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {M : Type*} [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]

members.closest_existing_considered: CategoryTheory.Tor / Tor' (Mathlib/CategoryTheory/Monoidal/Tor.lean) and Module.length (Mathlib/RingTheory/Length.lean), which are used as the building blocks; no Euler-characteristic-of-Tor definition exists in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib.
members.code:
noncomputable def intersectionMultiplicity (M N : Type u) [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]
    [AddCommGroup N] [Module R N] : ℤ :=
  ∑ᶠ i : ℕ, (-1 : ℤ) ^ i *
    (Module.length R
      (((Tor (ModuleCat.{u} R) i).obj (ModuleCat.of R M)).obj (ModuleCat.of R N))).toNat
members.docstring:
**Serre's intersection multiplicity** of two modules $M$ and $N$ over a commutative ring $R$:
$$\chi(M, N) := \sum_{i \ge 0} (-1)^i \ell_R(\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M, N)),$$
where $\ell_R$ denotes the length of an $R$-module.

This is meaningful when every $\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M, N)$ has finite length and only finitely
many of them are nonzero, e.g. when $R$ is a regular local ring (which has finite global
dimension), $M$ and $N$ are finitely generated and $M \otimes_R N$ has finite length. Outside of
this situation the value is a junk value: an infinite length is counted as $0$ (via `ENat.toNat`),
and a sum with infinitely many nonzero terms is $0$ (via `finsum`).
members.meaning: Σ_i (−1)^i ℓ(Tor_i^R(M, N)) as a finsum over all i.
members.name: intersectionMultiplicity
members.title: Serre's positivity conjecture
members.why: The representative truncates the alternating sum at an explicit extra parameter d (Finset.range (d+1)), whereas this variant takes a finsum over all i : ℕ, which is 0 whenever infinitely many Tor_i are nonzero (e.g. R = k[x]/(x²), M = N = k gives finsum 0 but truncated sum 1 for d = 0). Different arity and different values outside the regular-local case.

groups.notes: Both build χ(M,N) from CategoryTheory.Tor (ModuleCat R) and Module.length with ENat.toNat; they agree only under the additional hypothesis Tor_i^R(M,N) = 0 for i > d (e.g. R regular local of dimension d), which neither definition assumes. Neither notion exists in Mathlib.

groups.concept: set of crossings of a graph drawing
labels: set of crossings of a graph drawing

members.closest_existing_considered: No existing notion; Set.encard is used to count it (chosen over Set.ncard so infinite intersections give ⊤ rather than 0).
members.docstring:
The crossings of a drawing: an unordered pair of distinct edges together with a point of the
plane lying in the interior of both of their arcs.
members.meaning: The set of pairs (unordered pair of distinct edges, point) with the point in the interior of both arcs.
members.name: Drawing.crossings
members.title: Albertson conjecture

members.closest_existing_considered: No crossing-number notion exists in Mathlib or the repo (grep for 'crossing' finds only martingale upcrossings and category theory).
members.code:
def crossingSet : Set (Sym2 (Sym2 V) × ℝ²) :=
  {x | ¬ x.1.IsDiag ∧ x.2 ∉ Set.range D.vertex ∧ ∀ e ∈ x.1, D.OnEdge x.2 e}
members.docstring:
The crossings of the drawing `D`: an unordered pair of two *distinct* edges together with a
point of the plane that lies on the curves of both edges and is not a vertex. A point where `k`
edges meet therefore contributes `k.choose 2` crossings.
members.meaning: Pairs (unordered pair of distinct edges, non-vertex point) with the point on both edge curves.
members.name: crossingSet
members.title: Turán's brick factory problem
members.why: The two sets live in different types (`Set (Sym2 G.edgeSet × ℝ²)` vs `Set (Sym2 (Sym2 V) × ℝ²)`) and are built on different, file-local `Drawing` structures (arcs indexed by `G.edgeSet` vs curves `D.curve h` indexed by adjacency proofs `h : G.Adj u v`, whose structure is not even given here), so neither term can replace the other in the other file's statement. Mathematically the intended content agrees (interior points of both arcs ⇔ points on both curves that are not vertices, given the endpoint/interior axioms), so the cardinalities `encard` would coincide under a bijection, but the definitions themselves are not the same object.

groups.notes: Both are bespoke; Mathlib has no crossing-number notion. The variants agree in mathematical intent (a k-fold crossing point contributes k.choose 2 pairs, encard used to get ⊤ for infinitely many crossings) but differ in carrier type and in the underlying Drawing structure, so they are only equivalent up to a bijection, not interchangeable.

groups.concept: simple planar polygon region in ℝ³ (not necessarily convex)
labels: simple planar polygon region in ℝ³ (not necessarily convex)

members.closest_existing_considered: `convexHull ℝ` of a finite set (only convex polygons); `Affine.Simplex`/`Geometry.SimplicialComplex` (would force a fixed triangulation).
members.code:
def IsPolygon (f : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  (∃ s : Finset (Fin 3 → ℝ³), (∀ t ∈ s, AffineIndependent ℝ t) ∧
    f = ⋃ t ∈ s, convexHull ℝ (Set.range t)) ∧
  Module.finrank ℝ (affineSpan ℝ f).direction = 2 ∧
  Nonempty (f ≃ₜ Metric.closedBall (0 : ℝ²) 1)
members.docstring:
A (planar, not necessarily convex) *polygon* in `ℝ³`: a finite union of non-degenerate
triangles that lies in a plane (its affine span is two-dimensional) and is homeomorphic to a
closed disk. Equivalently, it is the region of a plane bounded by a simple closed polygonal
curve.
members.meaning: A finite union of nondegenerate triangles with 2-dimensional affine span, homeomorphic to a closed disk.
members.name: IsPolygon
members.title: Grünbaum's conjecture on spherical polyhedra that tile space by translation

members.closest_existing_considered: `convexHull ℝ (s : Finset ℝ³)` (convex only), `Geometry.SimplicialComplex` (triangles only, no grouping into planar faces), `EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon` in FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Geometry/2d.lean (2D, convex only).
members.code:
def IsPolygon (F : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  Coplanar ℝ F ∧
  Nonempty (F ≃ₜ Metric.closedBall (0 : ℝ²) 1) ∧
  ∃ E : Finset (ℝ³ × ℝ³), intrinsicFrontier ℝ F = ⋃ e ∈ E, segment ℝ e.1 e.2
members.docstring:
A set $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is a *polygon* (a simple, not necessarily convex, planar polygon
together with its interior) if it lies in a plane, is homeomorphic to a closed disk, and its
boundary relative to that plane is a finite union of line segments.
members.meaning: Coplanar set homeomorphic to a closed disk whose intrinsic frontier is a finite union of segments.
members.name: IsPolygon
members.title: Polyhedra with more than seven pairwise adjacent faces
members.why: Both say: planar set in ℝ³, homeomorphic to a closed disk, with polygonal boundary. A⇒B: finrank=2 gives Coplanar, and the frontier of a finite union of triangles in a plane is a finite union of (possibly degenerate) segments via the edge-line arrangement. B⇒A: a disk cannot embed in a line so the affine span is exactly 2-dimensional; by invariance of domain the intrinsic frontier is a polygonal Jordan curve, by the Jordan curve theorem F is the region it bounds, which triangulates into non-degenerate triangles. Equivalent, but the proof needs Jordan curve theorem / invariance of domain (not in Mathlib), so the Lean file below only states the equivalence with a `sorry`.

groups.notes: The two definitions are mathematically equivalent (same class of sets: closed planar polygonal disks in ℝ³, non-convex allowed, degenerate boundary segments in variant B are harmless since the frontier is a Jordan curve anyway; `Coplanar` (finrank ≤ 2) is upgraded to finrank = 2 by the disk homeomorphism). The equivalence proof, however, relies on invariance of domain, the Jordan curve theorem and polygon triangulation, none of which are in Mathlib, so the supplied check file states the `↔` but leaves the proof as `sorry`. Neither notion exists in Mathlib.

groups.concept: standard borromean rings (three mutually perpendicular ellipses)
labels: standard borromean rings (three mutually perpendicular ellipses)

members.closest_existing_considered: Nothing in Mathlib or the repo models any specific link or link diagram.
members.code: def borromeanRings : Set ℝ³ := ellipse₁ ∪ ellipse₂ ∪ ellipse₃
members.docstring:
The standard **Borromean rings**: the union of the three mutually perpendicular ellipses
`ellipse₁`, `ellipse₂`, `ellipse₃`, each with semi-axes `2` and `1`. The short axis of each
ellipse pierces the flat disk bounded by the next one (`ellipse₁` pierces the disk of `ellipse₂`
at $(0, \pm 1, 0)$, `ellipse₂` pierces the disk of `ellipse₃` at $(0, 0, \pm 1)$, and `ellipse₃`
pierces the disk of `ellipse₁` at $(\pm 1, 0, 0)$), while the long axis of each ellipse misses
the disk of the previous one. This is the configuration of the three golden rectangles inscribed
in a regular icosahedron, and it is the link `L6a4` (Alexander–Briggs `6³₂`).
members.meaning: Union of the three coordinate-plane ellipses with semi-axes 2 and 1 arranged cyclically.
members.name: borromeanRings
members.title: Borromean rings

members.closest_existing_considered: None in Mathlib or the repo
members.code: def borromeanRings : Set ℝ³ := ⋃ i, borromeanComponent i
members.docstring:
The standard configuration of the **Borromean rings**: three mutually perpendicular ellipses
with semi-axes `2` and `1`, one in each coordinate plane, with their major axes arranged
cyclically so that each ellipse passes through the disc spanned by the next one, see
`RopelengthProblems.borromeanComponent`. This is the ellipse version of the realization of the
Borromean rings by the three golden rectangles of a regular icosahedron.
members.meaning: Union of the three component ellipses.
members.name: borromeanRings
members.title: Ropelength problems
members.why: The indexed union ⋃ i : Fin 3 of borromeanComponent i unfolds (with i+1, i+2 mod 3) to exactly the three ellipses ellipse₁ (z=0, x²/4+y²=1), ellipse₂ (x=0, y²/4+z²=1), ellipse₃ (y=0, z²/4+x²=1), so the sets are equal; only the packaging (binary ∪ of three named sets vs ⋃ over Fin 3, conjunct order) differs, so it is provably equal but not by rfl.

groups.notes: Both files use the same standard realization (three mutually perpendicular ellipses with semi-axes 2 and 1 in the coordinate planes, cyclic major axes x,y,z). ℝ³ is assumed to be the same coordinate type (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) or Fin 3 → ℝ) in both files; the check works verbatim for either since only coordinate projections are used.

labels: subnormal subgroup

  Relation.ReflTransGen (fun A B : Subgroup G => A ≤ B ∧ (A.subgroupOf B).Normal) H ⊤
members.docstring:
A subgroup $H$ of $G$ is *subnormal* if there is a finite chain
$H = H_0 \trianglelefteq H_1 \trianglelefteq \dots \trianglelefteq H_n = G$ of subgroups, each
normal in the next.
members.meaning: There is a finite chain from H to G with each term normal in the next (reflexive-transitive closure).
members.name: IsSubnormal
members.title: Conjecture 7.15

members.closest_existing_considered: `Subgroup.Normal` (only normality in the whole group) and `(A.subgroupOf B).Normal` (single-step normality of A in B, used as the chain step); `Relation.ReflTransGen` reused to express the finite chain instead of an ad hoc inductive/Fin-indexed chain.
members.code:
def IsSubnormal (H : Subgroup G) : Prop :=
  Relation.ReflTransGen (fun A B : Subgroup G => A ≤ B ∧ (A.subgroupOf B).Normal) H ⊤
members.docstring:
A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is *subnormal*, written $H \lhd\lhd G$, if there is a finite chain
of subgroups $H = H_0 \lhd H_1 \lhd \dots \lhd H_n = G$ in which each $H_i$ is a normal subgroup
of $H_{i+1}$. Here "$A$ is a normal subgroup of $B$" is expressed as `A ≤ B` together with
`(A.subgroupOf B).Normal`.
members.meaning: There is a finite chain H = H₀ ⊴ H₁ ⊴ … ⊴ Hₙ = G of successive normal inclusions.
members.name: IsSubnormal
members.title: Conjecture 8.74
members.why: Same variable context {G : Type*} [Group G] and literally the same body: Relation.ReflTransGen (fun A B => A ≤ B ∧ (A.subgroupOf B).Normal) H ⊤.

groups.notes: Both files define subnormality identically via Relation.ReflTransGen over the step relation "A ≤ B ∧ (A.subgroupOf B).Normal" from H to ⊤. Mathlib has no notion of subnormal subgroup; this could be shared.

groups.concept: symplectic form on a manifold
labels: symplectic form
symplectic form on a manifold

members.closest_existing_considered: `extDerivWithin`, `ContDiffWithinAt` (used as ingredients); nothing symplectic exists.
members.code:
structure IsSymplecticForm (ω : TwoForm I M) : Prop where
  contDiffWithinAt : ∀ x₀ : M,
    ContDiffWithinAt ℝ ∞ (ω.localRep x₀) (Set.range I) (extChartAt I x₀ x₀)
  closed : ∀ x₀ : M, extDerivWithin (ω.localRep x₀) (Set.range I) (extChartAt I x₀ x₀) = 0
  nondegenerate : ∀ (x : M) (v : TangentSpace I x), (∀ w, ω x ![v, w] = 0) → v = 0
members.docstring:
A `2`-form `ω` on `M` is a **symplectic form** if it is smooth, closed and nondegenerate.
Smoothness and closedness (`dω = 0`) are expressed through the local representatives of `ω` in
the extended charts at each point, using Mathlib's exterior derivative `extDerivWithin` on the
model space.
members.meaning: A smooth, closed, nondegenerate 2-form (smoothness and closedness via local representatives).
members.name: IsSymplecticForm
members.title: Arnold–Givental conjecture and Arnold conjecture
variables:
variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  {H : Type*} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H)
  (M : Type*) [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M]

members.closest_existing_considered: `Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/SymplecticGroup.lean` (matrices only); `IsContMDiffRiemannianBundle` (symmetric positive case).
members.code:
structure IsSymplecticForm (Ω : SmoothBilinearForm I M) : Prop where
  skew : ∀ (x : M) (v w : TangentSpace I x), Ω x v w = - Ω x w v
  nondegenerate : ∀ (x : M) (v : TangentSpace I x), (∀ w : TangentSpace I x, Ω x v w = 0) → v = 0
  closed : ∀ (X Y Z : SmoothVectorField I M) (x : M), extDerivTwoForm I Ω X Y Z x = 0
members.docstring:
A smooth bilinear form `Ω` on the tangent bundle of `M` is a *symplectic form* if it is
skew-symmetric, nondegenerate and closed (`dΩ = 0`).
members.meaning: A smooth bilinear form on the tangent bundle that is pointwise skew-symmetric, nondegenerate, and closed (dΩ=0 on all smooth vector fields).
members.name: IsSymplecticForm
members.title: Weinstein conjecture
members.why: The predicates live on different types: the representative is a predicate on `TwoForm I M = ∀ x, TangentSpace I x [⋀^Fin 2]→L[ℝ] ℝ` (a not-necessarily-smooth family of alternating forms, with smoothness imposed via local chart representatives and no `IsManifold` hypothesis), whereas the variant is a predicate on `SmoothBilinearForm I M`, a smooth section `Cₛ^∞` of the bundle of (non-alternating) bilinear forms, requiring `[IsManifold I ∞ M]` and adding skew-symmetry as a field. Closedness is also expressed differently (chart-wise `extDerivWithin` of the local representative = 0 vs. the invariant Lie-bracket formula tested only against global smooth vector fields, which can be vacuous on manifolds with few global vector fields), so neither can replace the other in the other file's statement.

groups.notes: Both are bespoke 'symplectic form' notions absent from Mathlib, but they are formulated on incompatible carrier types (pointwise alternating 2-forms vs smooth sections of the bilinear-form bundle) and with different notions of closedness, so they are not interchangeable.

groups.concept: trace of frobenius of an elliptic curve over a number field at a finite place
labels: trace of frobenius of an elliptic curve over a number field at a finite place
trace of frobenius a_v = q_v + 1 − #ẽ(𝔽_v)

members.closest_existing_considered: ModularityConjecture.WeierstrassCurve.ap (not minimal-model based, wrong at bad primes, ℚ only)
members.docstring:
The number `a_v = q_v + 1 - #Ẽ(𝔽_v)`, where `#Ẽ(𝔽_v)` counts all the `𝔽_v`-points of the
reduced curve `Ẽ`: the affine solutions of the reduced Weierstrass equation together with the
point at infinity, including the singular point if there is one.

For a place of good reduction this is the trace of Frobenius. For a place of bad reduction it
equals `1`, `-1` or `0` according as the reduction is split multiplicative, non-split
multiplicative or additive.
members.meaning: q_v minus the number of affine solutions of the reduced equation (i.e. q_v + 1 − #Ẽ(𝔽_v) counting the point at infinity).
members.name: av
members.title: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture
variables:
variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [NumberField K] (E : WeierstrassCurve K)
  (v : HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))

members.code:
noncomputable def WeierstrassCurve.av (E : WeierstrassCurve K) (v : HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K)) :
    ℤ :=
  Ideal.absNorm v.asIdeal + 1 - numPointsReduction (v.valuation K).integer E
members.docstring:
The trace of Frobenius `a_v(E) = q_v + 1 - N_v` of a Weierstrass curve `E` over a number field
`K` at a finite place `v`, where `q_v` is the norm of `v` and `N_v` is the number of points over
the residue field of the reduction at `v` of a `v`-minimal model of `E`.
members.meaning: a_v = N(v) + 1 − N_v with N_v the point count of the reduction at v of a v-minimal model.
members.name: WeierstrassCurve.av
members.title: Sato–Tate conjecture
members.why: Both are q_v + 1 − (#affine points + 1) of the reduction of the same v-minimal model over the residue field of (v.valuation K).integer, with ℤ-subtraction; the representative writes q_v as Nat.card of the residue field of the valuation ring while the variant uses Ideal.absNorm v.asIdeal = Nat.card (𝓞 K ⧸ v.asIdeal). These agree since 𝓞 K → ResidueField 𝓞_{K,v} is surjective with kernel v.asIdeal, so the values coincide but not definitionally.

groups.notes: Both files rely on the same non-Mathlib helpers `WeierstrassCurve.minimal` / `WeierstrassCurve.reduction` (and on `IsDiscreteValuationRing`/`IsFractionRing` instances for `(v.valuation K).integer`) coming from their shared repo environment; the check file assumes those are available exactly as used in both sources. The mathematical content is identical (q_v + 1 − #Ẽ(𝔽_v) with the point at infinity counted, ℤ-subtraction); the only gap is q_v as `Nat.card (ResidueField 𝓞_{K,v})` vs `Ideal.absNorm v.asIdeal`, bridged in the check by proving 𝓞 K ⧸ v ≃+* ResidueField 𝓞_{K,v}. I could not compile the file here; the equivalence proof is complete in structure but individual Mathlib lemma names (e.g. `intValuation_le_pow_iff_dvd`, `Ideal.iInf_pow_eq_bot_of_isDomain`, `IsLocalRing.residue_eq_zero_iff`) may need minor adjustment to the exact Mathlib version.

groups.concept: trace of frobenius of an elliptic curve over ℚ at a prime
labels: trace of frobenius of an elliptic curve over ℚ at a prime

members.closest_existing_considered: ModularityConjecture.WeierstrassCurve.ap (not importable from a problem file; uses a cruder reduction).
members.code:
noncomputable def WeierstrassCurve.apRat (E : WeierstrassCurve ℚ) (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] : ℤ :=
  p + 1 - numPointsReduction ℤ_[p] (E.baseChange ℚ_[p])
members.docstring:
The trace of Frobenius `a_p(E) = p + 1 - N_p` of a Weierstrass curve `E` over `ℚ` at a prime
`p`, where `N_p` is the number of points over `𝔽_p` of the reduction modulo `p` of a minimal model
of `E` at `p`.
members.meaning: a_p = p + 1 − N_p where N_p counts points of the reduction mod p of a minimal model of E ⊗ ℚ_p over ℤ_p.
members.name: WeierstrassCurve.apRat
members.title: Sato–Tate conjecture

members.closest_existing_considered: ModularityConjecture.WeierstrassCurve.ap in FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/ModularityConjecture.lean — rejected because it reduces the rational coefficients naively (no minimal model, wrong at non-integral models / bad primes) and omits the point at infinity by convention.
members.code:
noncomputable def frobeniusTrace : ℤ :=
  p + 1 - Nat.card (reductionAt E p).toAffine.Point
members.docstring:
The trace of Frobenius `a_p(E) = p + 1 - #Ẽ(𝔽_p)` of `E` at `p`, where `Ẽ` is the reduction
of `E` modulo `p` and `#Ẽ(𝔽_p)` counts the nonsingular affine points together with the point at
infinity.
members.meaning: a_p = p + 1 − #Ẽ(F_p), with the point count the Nat.card of the affine points (including infinity) of the reduction of a minimal model.
members.name: frobeniusTrace
members.title: Supersingular primes
members.why: Both reduce the same curve ((E.baseChange ℚ_[p]).minimal ℤ_[p]).reduction ℤ_[p], but apRat counts all affine solutions of the Weierstrass equation (+1 for infinity) while frobeniusTrace uses Nat.card of Mathlib's Affine.Point, which only contains Nonsingular affine points (+zero). They agree at primes of good reduction but at bad primes the reduced cubic has a rational singular point, so apRat = frobeniusTrace - 1 there (e.g. split multiplicative: 0 vs 1).

groups.notes: The two definitions agree exactly on primes of good reduction (where every affine solution is nonsingular), which is all that Sato–Tate / supersingular-prime statements actually use, but as total functions on all primes they differ at bad primes.

groups.concept: unknot (trivial knot)
labels: unknot (trivial knot)
unknot (subset ambient isotopic to a round circle)

members.closest_existing_considered: IsEmbedding γ for γ : Circle → ℝ³ (used in InscribedSquare.lean) gives simple closed curves but says nothing about being unknotted.
members.code:
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ C, IsRoundCircle C ∧ AmbientIsotopic K C
members.docstring:
A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an **unknotted space curve** (an unknot) if it is ambient isotopic to
a round circle. Such a set is automatically a tame simple closed curve, i.e. the image of a
topological embedding of the circle.
members.meaning: There is a round circle to which the set is ambient isotopic.
members.name: IsUnknot
members.title: Borromean rings

members.closest_existing_considered: `Homeomorph` (used); Mathlib has no knot equivalence, isotopy or Reidemeister moves.
members.code: def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardCircle
members.docstring:
A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an *unknot* (a trivial knot) if some homeomorphism of `ℝ³` maps it
onto the standard circle. The homeomorphism is not required to preserve orientation: the
standard circle is preserved by the reflection `p 2 ↦ -p 2`, so this is the same as asking for
an orientation preserving homeomorphism, or for an ambient isotopy. For polygonal knots this is
equivalent (by Dehn's lemma) to the piecewise-linear notion used by Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger:
the knot can be deformed, through simple polygons, to a planar polygon.
members.meaning: A subset of ℝ³ carried onto the standard circle by some homeomorphism of ℝ³.
members.name: IsUnknot
members.title: Unknotting problem
members.why: Same predicate on subsets of ℝ³ but not by unfolding: the representative asks for an ambient isotopy from the identity onto some round circle (any centre/plane/radius), the variant asks for a single homeomorphism (possibly orientation‑reversing, no isotopy) onto the fixed unit circle in the xy‑plane. 1⇒2 is elementary (compose H 1 with the similarity taking the round circle to the standard circle); 2⇒1 uses that the reflection p 2 ↦ -p 2 fixes the standard circle together with the deep theorem that every orientation‑preserving homeomorphism of ℝ³ is isotopic to the identity (Fisher 1960 / Moise–Bing), so the notions coincide only via nontrivial 3‑manifold topology.

groups.notes: Both files presumably use ℝ³ := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3). The two definitions are extensionally the same predicate, but only via a deep theorem (connectedness of Homeo⁺(ℝ³), Fisher 1960 / Moise–Bing) plus the reflection trick; the check file cannot be closed without sorry because Mathlib has none of this 3‑manifold topology. If a purely formal (Mathlib‑provable) equivalence is required, treat the relation as 'different in form, equivalent in mathematics'.

groups.concept: verbal subgroup of the free group of countable rank determined by a set of words (consequences of laws)
labels: verbal subgroup of the free group of countable rank determined by a set of words (consequences of laws)

members.closest_existing_considered: `Subgroup.closure`, `Subgroup.normalClosure` (only closes under conjugation, not under all endomorphisms, so it does not capture consequences of laws).
members.code:
def verbalClosure (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : Subgroup (FreeGroup ℕ) :=
  Subgroup.closure {w | ∃ s ∈ S, ∃ φ : FreeGroup ℕ →* FreeGroup ℕ, φ s = w}
members.docstring:
The verbal subgroup of $F_\infty$ determined by a set $S$ of words: the subgroup generated
by all values of the words in $S$ on elements of $F_\infty$, i.e. by all images of elements of
$S$ under endomorphisms of $F_\infty$. This is the fully invariant closure of $S$, and its
elements are exactly the consequences of the identical relations in $S$.
members.meaning: The subgroup of FreeGroup ℕ generated by all images of the given words under endomorphisms of FreeGroup ℕ (fully invariant closure).
members.name: verbalClosure
members.title: Conjecture 1.86

members.closest_existing_considered: Subgroup.closure / Subgroup.normalClosure (not endomorphism-closed, so insufficient on their own); Mathlib has no verbal/fully invariant subgroup notion.
members.code:
def verbalSubgroup (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : Subgroup (FreeGroup ℕ) :=
  Subgroup.closure {w | ∃ s ∈ S, ∃ φ : FreeGroup ℕ →* FreeGroup ℕ, φ s = w}
members.docstring:
The verbal subgroup of `FreeGroup ℕ` determined by a set of words `S`: the subgroup
generated by all images of elements of `S` under endomorphisms of `FreeGroup ℕ`. Its
elements are exactly the consequences of the words in `S`, i.e. the words that are
identities of every group in which all words of `S` are identities.
members.meaning: The subgroup of FreeGroup ℕ generated by all endomorphic images of the words in S, i.e. the consequences of S.
members.name: verbalSubgroup
members.title: Conjecture 1.87
members.why: Both are `Subgroup.closure {w | ∃ s ∈ S, ∃ φ : FreeGroup ℕ →* FreeGroup ℕ, φ s = w}` on `S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)`; the bodies are character-for-character the same apart from the name.

groups.notes: Both files define the verbal subgroup of FreeGroup ℕ determined by S as the subgroup closure of all endomorphic images of elements of S; the definitions coincide syntactically. Mathlib has no verbal/fully invariant subgroup notion.

groups.concept: virtually polycyclic group (polycyclic-by-finite)
labels: virtually polycyclic group (polycyclic-by-finite)

members.closest_existing_considered: Group.IsVirtuallyNilpotent (pattern copied, but wrong property).
members.code:
def IsVirtuallyPolycyclic (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ H : Subgroup G, IsPolycyclic H ∧ H.FiniteIndex
members.docstring:
A group $G$ is *almost polycyclic* (or *virtually polycyclic*, or *polycyclic-by-finite*)
if it has a polycyclic subgroup of finite index.
members.meaning: The group has a polycyclic subgroup of finite index (normality not required, but equivalent via the normal core).
members.name: IsVirtuallyPolycyclic
members.title: Conjecture 1.31

members.closest_existing_considered: `Subgroup.FiniteIndex` and `Subgroup.Normal` (used as building blocks); no combined notion exists.
members.code:
def IsPolycyclicByFinite (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ (P : Subgroup G) (_ : P.Normal), IsPolycyclic P ∧ P.FiniteIndex
members.docstring: A group is *polycyclic-by-finite* if it has a polycyclic normal subgroup of finite index.
members.meaning: There is a normal polycyclic subgroup of finite index.
members.name: IsPolycyclicByFinite
members.title: Conjecture 5.5

groups.concept: π-group for a set of primes π (periodic with element orders having prime divisors in π)
labels: π-group for a set of primes π (periodic with element orders having prime divisors in π)

members.closest_existing_considered: IsPGroup p G (single prime only); Nat.primeFactors/Nat.factorization (would silently treat orderOf = 0 as having no prime factors).
members.code:
def IsPiGroup (π : Set Nat.Primes) : Prop :=
  ∀ g : G, IsOfFinOrder g ∧ ∀ p : Nat.Primes, (p : ℕ) ∣ orderOf g → p ∈ π
members.docstring:
For a set $\pi$ of primes, a group is a *$\pi$-group* if every element has finite order
and every prime dividing the order of an element lies in $\pi$.
members.meaning: Every element has finite order and all primes dividing that order belong to π.
members.name: IsPiGroup
members.title: Conjecture 3.12

members.closest_existing_considered: IsPGroup p G (single prime; a π-group is not a conjunction/disjunction of these).
members.code:
def IsPiGroup (π : Set Nat.Primes) (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ g : G, IsOfFinOrder g ∧ ∀ p : Nat.Primes, (p : ℕ) ∣ orderOf g → p ∈ π
members.docstring:
For a set of primes `π`, a group `G` is a *`π`-group* if every element of `G` has finite order
and every prime divisor of the order of every element of `G` lies in `π`.
members.meaning: Every element has finite order and all primes dividing that order lie in π.
members.name: IsPiGroup
members.title: Conjecture 8.14
members.why: The bodies are literally the same term (∀ g, IsOfFinOrder g ∧ ∀ p : Nat.Primes, (p:ℕ) ∣ orderOf g → p ∈ π); the only difference is the order of the explicit arguments G and π, which is cosmetic.

groups.notes: Both files define the same notion; the definitions coincide syntactically up to argument order. Mathlib has only IsPGroup for a single prime, so this bespoke π-group definition is genuinely not in Mathlib.

groups.concept: 𝔛-radical of a group for a class 𝔛 (join of normal 𝔛-subgroups)
labels: x-radical of a group (join of normal subgroups belonging to a class)
𝔛-radical of a group for a class 𝔛 (join of normal 𝔛-subgroups)

members.closest_existing_considered: Nothing in Mathlib: only ring-theoretic radicals (Ideal.radical, nilradical, Jacobson) and Koethe radical in the repo; no group-class radical.
members.code:
def radical (G : Type u) [Group G] : Subgroup G :=
  sSup {N : Subgroup G | N.Normal ∧ 𝔛 N}
members.docstring:
The `𝔛`-radical `𝔛(G)` of a group `G`: the join of all normal subgroups of `G` that belong
to the class `𝔛`. For a radical class `𝔛` this is the largest normal `𝔛`-subgroup of `G`.
members.meaning: The supremum of all normal subgroups belonging to the class.
members.name: radical
members.title: Conjecture 3.45

members.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib has no radical for classes of groups; `Subgroup.normalCore`, `commutator` etc. are unrelated.
members.code:
def radical (𝔛 : GroupClass) (G : Type) [Group G] : Subgroup G :=
  sSup {N : Subgroup G | N.Normal ∧ GrpCat.of N ∈ 𝔛}
members.docstring:
The $\mathfrak{X}$-radical $G_{\mathfrak{X}}$ of a group $G$: the join of all normal
subgroups of $G$ that belong to the class $\mathfrak{X}$. When $\mathfrak{X}$ is a Fitting class
and $G$ is finite, this is the largest normal $\mathfrak{X}$-subgroup of $G$.
members.meaning: The join of all normal subgroups of G that belong to the class 𝔛; the 𝔛-radical G_𝔛.
members.name: radical
members.title: Conjecture 8.30
members.why: Same informal recipe (sSup of {N | N.Normal ∧ N ∈ 𝔛}), but the class parameter has a different formal type — 8.30 uses `GroupClass := Set GrpCat.{0}` with membership `GrpCat.of N ∈ 𝔛`, whereas 3.45 applies `𝔛 : GroupClass.{u}` directly to the subgroup as a type (`𝔛 N`), i.e. a universe-polymorphic predicate on groups — and the ambient group is `G : Type` (universe 0) in 8.30 versus `G : Type u` in 3.45. Neither definition can be substituted for the other without changing the type of 𝔛 and the universe of quantification.

groups.notes: Mathematically both are the 𝔛-radical (join of normal 𝔛-subgroups); the difference is purely in the encoding of the class 𝔛 (Set of bundled GrpCat.{0} objects vs. a predicate on Type u groups) and in the universe of G. Mathlib has no such notion.
